It should be emphasized that dosage and the upper limits of adaptation are the 
biggest problems in the transmutation mesocycle. In this training cycle the highest 
sport-specific workloads are concentrated.  Execution of these workloads substantially 

===== IDX 121 (printed 110) =====
110
 
 
determines each athlete's individual progress. However, it is very difficult to 
determine the upper limit of adaptation that athletes should not exceed. Even 
evaluation of the hormonal state and other blood markers does not unequivocally 
guarantee a timely diagnosis of overtraining.  
 
One of the most comprehensive definitions of overtraining was given by ex-
world record holder and Olympic champion runner and sport physiologist, Peter 
Snell.  He stated that, “Overtraining may be regarded as a state in which performance 
diminishes while the level of training is maintained or increased” (Snell, 1990). 
According to this explanation, the person who makes decisions about overtraining is 
the coach. From the coach's viewpoint, it is very important to recognize the generally 
accepted warning signals of the early phases of overtraining such as: (1) an increase in 
resting HR of more than 5 beats/min over a three-five day period; (2) persistent or 
rapid decrease of body mass; (3) persistent increased rate of general fatigue; (4) 
persistent increased rate of muscle soreness; (5) persistent increased rate of sleep 
disturbances (Burke et al., 1990; Hooper et al., 1995). 
 
 
Case study. Nineteen elite swimmers were monitored during a 6-month period 
of preparation using a large battery of blood and urine markers, hormones, CPK, 
resting blood pressure and HR, and event-specific all-out tests with blood lactate 
determination. In addition, all swimmers made daily entries in their log-books of 
swim volume, time of dry-land workout and subjective ratings of stress, fatigue, 
sleep quality and muscle soreness on a scale of 1 (very, very low or good) to 7 
(very, very high or bad). During the study three athletes were diagnosed as 
overtrained. However, the difference between stale and non-stale swimmers was 
not reflected in any blood, urine or other markers during mid- or late-season. 
Nevertheless, the differences were revealed quite significantly through fatigue 
and muscle soreness ratings. Moreover, the multi-component statistical model 
embracing the mean ratings of stress, fatigue, sleep quality and muscle soreness 
was able to predict changes in competitive performance. Interestingly, the use of 
a larger battery of indicators did not increase the accuracy of prediction (Hooper 
et al., 1995)       
 

===== IDX 122 (printed 111) =====
111
 
 
 
This example shows that sometimes even simple inexpensive methods (i.e. 
subjective ratings of stress, fatigue, sleep quality and muscle soreness), if used 
systematically and responsibly, provide effective monitoring of training that is 
particularly desirable in the high-load transmutation mesocycle.    
 
 
3.2.3. Realization mesocycle  
 
 
Traditionally, the realization mesocycle is termed the taper. In traditional 
periodization the taper is used prior to important competitions and is intended to 
stimulate better performance. According to the Block Periodization concept, the 
realization mesocycle forms the concluding phase of each training stage and, 
therefore, its function is broader. It is directed to attaining peak-performance and thus 
does not differ from the usual tapering technique. However, this mesocycle also 
concludes a carefully designed program consisting of several training stages in which 
all the important components are intentionally developed (see Figure 1.8).  
 
The training stages in early- mid- and late season are not identical. 
Correspondingly, the realization mesocycles also differ depending on the level and 
importance of the forthcoming competition.  This determines the essential 
characteristics of the mesocycle such as its duration, reduction of workloads, 
emotional tension of athletes, etc. These particulars are summarized in Table 3.12 and 
are considered briefly.  
 
The transmutation mesocycle, in which maximal amounts of workloads are 
performed leads into the realization mesocycle. Consequently, athletes start the 
mesocycle when they are fatigued. Because of this the first objective is to provide and 
facilitate restoration and ultimately to attain the supercompensation state at the time of 
competition. It is important to remember that the targeted abilities, which should be 
the focus of the mesocycle program, demand high sensitivity and reactivity of the 
central and peripheral nervous systems, availability of energy resources and mental 
concentration. These prerequisites for proper development are seen in well rested 
athletes. Therefore, reduction of workload level is of paramount importance at the 
initiation of the realization program.

There are different approaches as to how the workloads can be reduced. The 
salient factor that affects the rate of workload reduction is duration of the mesocycle. 
A short mesocycle demands a fast workload decrease, a more prolonged mesocycle 
can be planned with a gradual reduction of workload level. The duration itself, is 
extremely important and sensitive. A long-duration mesocycle can lead athletes to 
detraining while an excessively short mesocycle may not be sufficient to restore and 
develop event-specific abilities. This contradiction was specifically noted (Mujika et 
al., 2004).

Simulation and enhancement of techno-tactical competitive behavior is an 
obligatory component of the realization mesocycle in many sports. Despite the 
striking specificity of various sports, the general idea of techno-tactical simulation is 
very similar – adjusting athletes to the planned or expected competitive behavior. 
Consequently, techno-tactical simulation programs should meet the following 
demands: (1) the competitive situation (race pattern, tactical combination, techno-
tactical task etc.)  should as closely reproduced as possible in the exercise; (2) the 
level of athletes’ concentration should approximate competitive levels; and (3) the 
number of simulations should be sufficient to attain stable and reliable techno-tactical 
skills. The typical techno-tactical tasks and their dosage in the realization mesocycle 
for qualified kayakers are presented in Table 3.13

Emotional tension and anxiety are attributes of pre-event preparation.  Their 
occurrence is seen mostly later in the season, when the importance of the competitions 
and the need to do well in them is greatest.  Keep in mind the contradictory impact of 
pre-event tapering on the emotional state of athletes. There is considerable evidence 
that workload reduction during the taper causes a remarkable improvement in mood 
associated mainly with improved recovery (see review by Mujika et al., 2004). 
However, pre-competition anxiety can change this trend dramatically at least in terms 
of two general factors: (1) a moderate level of anxiety facilitates performance and 
positively affects athletes’ behavior, while excessive anxiety detracts from 
performance; (2) the effects of such emotional stimulation depend on the athletes’

identical, the similarity of the monitoring programs provides a number of visible 
benefits for athlete preparation: 
- 
The coach can select, check and validate the entire set of tests and indicators; 
-

-

more stressful situations as the target competition approaches; 
-

necessary) can be determined in advance and adjusted individually.

Nutrition during the realization mesocycle should be given special attention 
especially in regard to balancing dietary intake and energy expenditure. As was 
emphasized, workload reduction is characteristic of this mesocycle. Correspondingly, 
energy expenditure decreases significantly while athletes' nutritional habits often 
remain unchanged. As a result, energy intake can surpass energy expenditure causing 
a noticeable increase in the fat component.  
 
 
Case study. Twenty highly qualified male long-distance triathletes were 
monitored during a four-week mesocycle with high workloads and a subsequent 
two-week taper mesocycle with reduced workloads. Body mass, body fat, energy 
intake and expenditure were evaluated. It was found that the average energy 
intake remained at the same level, but energy expenditure decreased during the 
taper mesocycle by up to 69.3% (Figure 3.10).  Mean body mass of the group 
didn’t change but body fat mass increased by 4.3%. The imbalance of dietary 
intake and energy expenditure caused remarkable fat accumulation. However, it is 
also possible that their muscle mass decreased as well while body mass remained 
at the previous level. Therefore, body mass as an indicator of the anthropometric 
state, is not always reliable.  The pre-competition reduction of training workloads 
requires attention to nutrition, which should correspond to the decreased energy 
expenditure (based on Margaritis et al., 2003).

In conclusion, the realization mesocycle definitely has the lowest level of 
workloads but the level of emotional tension can be much higher than during the usual 
training routine. Consequently, this emotional factor can substantially modify both the 
athletes’ behavior and training responses.  
 
3.3. Training stage 
 
According to Block Periodization, three consecutive mesocycle-blocks form a 
single training stage. Its length depends on the duration of each mesocycle and varies 
from 4-10 weeks.  As was already noted (1.2.3), the training stage reconstructs the 
entire annual cycle in miniature.  This allows for the consecutive development of 
basic abilities (as in the preparatory period), specific abilities (as in the competitive 
period), and integrative readiness for event-specific performance. The most favorable 
carry-over of residual training effects makes it possible to attain the optimal 
combination of basic, special and event-specific abilities as needed at the moment of 
competition (Figure 1.8). However, if the training design is based solely on the length 
of training residuals, it will be extremely rigid and inflexible. There are also other 
factors influencing training residuals and additional methods to prolong them.   
 

===== IDX 128 (printed 117) =====
117
 
 
3.3.1. Competition in the training stage.   
 
 
It is well known that not all competitions are planned for peak performance. 
Some of them include extraordinarily high workloads to break the training routine and 
to add emotional diversity to the preparation. With this aim in mind, competition can 
be included in the accumulation and transmutation mesocycles. However, their 
influence is unequivocal. Highly intense competitions produce profound physical and 
emotional stress. The secretion of stress hormones like catecholamines and cortisol, 
modulate the athletes’ metabolic response and reinforce the catabolic process (Viru & 
Viru, 2001). As a result, muscle mass and maximum strength can decrease.  
 
Moreover, the highly intense anaerobic glycolitic efforts typical in competition 
suppress the activity of aerobic enzymes and the oxidative process in the 
mitochondria (Volkov, 1986).  This impairment of aerobic fitness has been noted for 
some time by prominent coaches rather intuitively.  They added special aerobic 
workloads to restore and revitalize the athletes after competition. A recent publication 
elucidates this negative effect of competition because of the shortened training 
residuals (Issurin & Lustig, 2004).  
  
Case study.  The preparation of multi- Olympic and World swimming 
champion Alexandre Popov was monitored using an incremental stepwise 
swimming test. His anaerobic threshold speed was determined at a blood lactate 
level of 4 mM and a speed producing 8 mM, as the lower limit of highly intense 
glycolitic workloads. These indicators were evaluated at the beginning of the 
mesocycle with highly concentrated aerobic workloads, ten days after this 
evaluation, and a few days after the competition in which Alexandre performed 
several times (Figure 3.11). In the initial stage of this study the remarkable gain 
in both anaerobic threshold speed and speed corresponding to 8 mM was noted. 
However, upon measurement of these factors again after competition, a 
substantial decrease was seen.  This can be attributed to shortened training 
residuals, induced by the previous program (adapted from Pyne & 
Touretski,1993).

To conclude this section, the following relevant factors are worth noting: 
1) Incorporating mid- and low-level competitions in the training stage is an 
important and meaningful component of the entire preparation; 
2) Competitive performances elicit superior and profound athletes’ responses that 
enrich the spectrum of adaptation to the training routine.  However; 
3) Highly intense competitive efforts bring about secretion of stress hormones 
that modulate metabolic and hormonal responses and shorten the residual 
training effects of the preceding mesocycle. This should be taken into account 
in the subsequent program.  
 
3.3.2.  How to prolong the residual training effects 
 
 
Inasmuch as the training stage is a sequence of three mesocycle-blocks, the 
crucial factor that restricts the length of a particular stage is the duration of the 
residual training effects after the first accumulation mesocycle which lasts about 30 
days (Table 1.6). This timing determines the total duration of the second and third 
mesocycles, which should not be longer than the training residuals of the aerobic and 
strength workloads, i.e., one month. However, in many sports the transmutation 

===== IDX 130 (printed 119) =====
119
 
 
mesocycle is directed at reinforcing anaerobic glycolitic abilities, which takes three-
four weeks.  In addition, the duration of the realization mesocycle (taper) can last 
about two weeks. The duration of both of these mesocycles (about five weeks) 
exceeds the time of the strength-aerobic training residuals that may cause the athletes 
to approach the targeted competition at a reduced level of basic abilities.  
 
It is obvious that some special measures should be undertaken to prolong the 
training residuals of the strength-aerobic program. This prolongation can be attained 
by additional supporting workouts for aerobic endurance and/or muscular strength. 
But, such additions are not successful. The highly intense transmutation mesocycle 
strongly suppresses the immediate effect of aerobic training and the anabolic strength 
exercises require sufficient recovery that cannot be provided. Apparently, what should 
be inserted in the mesocycle is not several additional workouts but a special compact 
mini-block (short microcycle), in order to prolong training residuals. This principal 
approach is displayed in Figure 3.12.

===== IDX 131 (printed 120) =====
120
 
 
Example. Imagine a situation in which two targeted competitions have a 
five-week interval between them (this situation is very typical for kayaking 
where the European and World championships are separated by an interval of 
five-six weeks). In this case of inflexible time limits, you can plan 10-14 days for 
accumulation, 10-14 days for transmutation, and 8-10 days for the realization 
mesocycles. Here you need not include mini-blocks because the training 
residuals following the accumulation mesocycle surpass the competition. 
Another situation occurs when you are forced to plan a training stage for a period 
of 7-9 weeks (this situation is very typical of pre-Olympic preparation in several 
sports where the international calendar has no competitions scheduled before the 
major event). In this case, it is reasonable to plan longer mesocycles and the 
inclusion of mini-blocks would be necessary.    
  
 
Summary 
Microcycles, as the shortest training cycles, are differentiated in three 
principle ways, loading, competing and recovery. The microcycles devoted to loading 
differ according to load level. There is adjustment that serves to adapt athletes to 
increasing workloads, loading that is used to develop athletic abilities, and impact that 
employs extreme training stimuli. The competing microcycle contains the pre-
competitive microcycle, which prepares the athlete for forthcoming competitions and 
the competitive microcycle, where the athlete takes part in the competition. The 
recovery microcycle consists of a special restoration microcycle. The microcycles can 
be managed with respect to different load variations. More specifically, one-, two-, 
and three-peak designs can be executed.  
 
Presented in this chapter are microcycles focusing on (a) aerobic (strength-
aerobic) abilities, (b) highly intense anaerobic workloads, (c) explosive strength in 
highly coordinated exercises, and (d) pre-competitive training. These microcycles 
have guidelines for structuring the microcycle. A number of general rules for 
constructing the microcycle are as follows: (1) priority of the most meaningful key-
workouts (2) interaction of successive workouts (3) sharing of restoration means (4) 
initiating and peaking training workloads, and (5) monitoring the training.  
 
 

===== IDX 132 (printed 121) =====
121
 
 
The three types of mesocycles proposed by the Block Periodization Concept 
are considered with respect to duration, content and monitoring of training. 
Specifically, the accumulation, transmutation and realization mesocycles are 
described with respect to the sequencing of various microcycles.  Also covered is 
fatigue accumulation that is particularly pronounced in the transmutation mesocycle, 
the selection of appropriate tasks and exercises, and determination of the most 
adequate means of monitoring several mesocycles. It is important to remember that 
athletes’ self-estimation of training response in their log-book can provide valuable 
information for preventing excessive fatigue and even overtraining. Subjective ratings 
of stress, fatigue, quality of sleep and muscle soreness on a scale of 1 (very, very low 
or good) to 7 (very, very high or bad) are recommended for systematic use.  
 
 
The training stage, consisting of three sequenced mesocycles, reconstructs the 
annual cycle in miniature, where training stimuli are focused first on basic abilities, 
second on more specific abilities, and third on integrative readiness for event-specific 
performance. It is essential to remember that competitive performances and emotional 
strain can shorten the training residuals of the preceding mesocycle.  This 
phenomenon was considered through a case-study example of multi- Olympic 
champion Alexander Popov, whose anaerobic threshold speed decreased significantly 
after competition. Inclusion of special compact mini-blocks (short microcycles) can 
prolong the residual training effects of the preceding mesocycle. Thus, aerobic mini-
blocks can be inserted in the transmutation mesocycle and a highly intense anaerobic 
mini-block can be incorporated within the realization mesocycle.

    13	
    14	# Six Microcycle Types by Purpose and Load, With One-, Two-, and Three-Peak Weekly Load Waves
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Table 3.1 (PDF p. 88, printed p. 77; verified against the page image)
    17	gives six microcycle types, each with a stated purpose, load level, design particular, and
    18	duration range: **Adjustment** (initial adaptation to loads, medium load, gradual workload
    19	increase, **5-7 days**); **Loading** (fitness development, substantial-high load, big/substantial
    20	workloads, **5-9 days**); **Impact** (fitness development via extreme stimuli, very
    21	high-extreme load, summation of extreme workloads, **4-7 days**); **Pre-competitive**
    22	(immediate preparation for competition, medium load, tuning with event-specific means,
    23	**5-7 days**, see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] for full detail);
    24	**Competitive** (participation in competition, high-very high load, sport/event-specific
    25	performance, **2-7 days**); **Restoration** (active recovery, low load, wide spectrum of
    26	restorative means, **3-7 days**). Issurin notes the adjustment microcycle can shorten to
    27	3-5 days mid-season (e.g., starting a new training stage or a camp), and the restoration
    28	microcycle after camp or competition typically runs 3-4 days mid-season (PDF p. 88, printed
    29	p. 77). Separately, Issurin describes load variation **within** a microcycle as a "wave-shape
    30	design" using the 5-point load scale from [[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]]:
    31	Figure 3.1 (PDF p. 90, printed p. 79) shows one-, two-, and three-peak weekly load patterns
    32	for single-workout-per-day microcycles. Two- and three-peak designs are described as "used
    33	most widely" because they let athletes handle a relatively large weekly workload with reduced
    34	excessive-fatigue risk; the one-peak design concentrates several developmental workouts for a
    35	"more profound and stressful training response," a pattern reserved for "sufficiently
    36	prepared high-performance athletes" and not for novices. For microcycles with two workouts
    37	per day, Figure 3.2 (PDF p. 91, printed p. 80) gives a worked ten-workout example: two
    38	development workouts open the week (first peak), two medium-load supporting workouts
    39	provide restoration, then a three-session mini-block including two key-workouts forms the
    40	second peak, with the week's final session usable as a time-trial or scrimmage.
    41	
    42	**Why it works** — Issurin frames the point-scale quantification (adapted from the 5-point
    43	load scale) as serving three purposes: it lets coaches in non-measurable sports (sailing,
    44	team/dual sports) express load numerically and visually; it lets athletes see and
    45	consciously anticipate key-workouts and the restoration that follows load peaks
    46	(a didactic use); and it lets whole microcycles be compared to each other for planning
    47	purposes (PDF pp. 91-92, printed pp. 80-81). The peak/trough pattern itself follows the same
    48	general logic as [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]: concentrating the
    49	week's hardest sessions into one, two, or three peaks (rather than spreading maximal effort
    50	evenly across every day) lets fatigue clear between peaks so each peak can still be
    51	performed at a high standard.
    52	
    53	**When to apply** — Classifying a week's purpose before assigning workouts to it (is this
    54	week meant to adjust athletes to new load, develop fitness, deliver an extreme stimulus, tune
    55	for competition, compete, or actively recover), and then shaping that week's daily load curve
    56	around one, two, or three peaks depending on athlete level and the week's targeted abilities.
    57	**Inference, mapped to a college football calendar:** early fall camp days function like
    58	Issurin's **adjustment** microcycle (medium load, gradual ramp, until two-a-days are
    59	tolerated); the heaviest camp week(s) resemble the **impact** type (very high-extreme load,
    60	short duration, 4-7 days, matching the "impact week" concept sometimes used informally in
    61	strength-staff planning); the week of the season opener and each bowl-prep week function as
    62	**pre-competitive** microcycles (see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]]); a
    63	normal in-season game week is Issurin's **competitive** microcycle in form (the whole week
    64	organized around one **competition**, 2-7 days), though its internal training content is
    65	closer to what [[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] describes; and a bye
    66	week or the week after a game before a short turnaround functions as a **restoration**
    67	microcycle. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name these six categories explicitly, but
    68	the general planning language ("a 'training week' does not have to equal 7 calendar days,"
    69	`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing week1-lecture.md p.39) is
    70	consistent with treating microcycle type, not just calendar week, as the planning unit.
    71	
    72	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The six-type table's specific duration ranges are
    73	Issurin's own applied categorization; no citation or derivation is given for why, e.g., the
    74	loading type is 5-9 days rather than some other range. **Inference:** none of the six types
    75	or the one-/two-/three-peak wave figures are demonstrated on a team-sport example in this
    76	section (that comes later, 3.1.7); the load-wave figures here are drawn from individual/dual
    77	sport contexts, and the specific number-of-peaks guidance ("one-peak... not [for] novice and
    78	less prepared athletes") is stated for individual-sport training loads, not validated for a
    79	100+ player roster with heterogeneous training ages. The point-scale system inherits every
    80	limitation already logged for the underlying RPE/restoration-time scale in
    81	[[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]] (subjective, no cited validation
    82	of the specific cut-points).
    83	
    84	**Example** — A four-week fall-camp block could be read as adjustment (days 1-5, single
    85	practices, medium load) into loading (days 6-14, one-a-days plus early two-a-days) into an
    86	impact microcycle (the hardest stretch of two-a-days, 4-7 days) into a pre-competitive
    87	microcycle in the week before the opener, each transition marked by a deliberate change in
    88	purpose and load level, not just a generic "camp is getting harder" narrative.
    89	
    90	**Related** — [[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]] (the 5-point scale
    91	this section's point-quantification is built on), [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]],
    92	[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]],
    93	[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]],
    94	[[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]].

    14	# Popov's Aerobic Microcycle: Anaerobic Glycolytic Work Is Nearly Absent Even for a 100m Freestyle Sprinter
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Issurin presents Alexander Popov's (Russia, multi-Olympic/World 50-100m
    17	Freestyle swimming champion) typical strength-aerobic microcycle from his preparatory phase
    18	(the accumulation mesocycle, in Block Periodization terms) as an example (PDF pp. 92-94,
    19	printed pp. 81-83, Figure 3.3 and Table 3.2; sourced to "courtesy of Gennadi Touretski,
    20	personal communication," Popov's coach). Across ten workouts, anaerobic threshold (AT) work
    21	and technical stroke-count drills dominated; maximal-speed (alactic) exercises appeared daily
    22	in medium proportions; aerobic power (AP) work appeared in only three workouts; strength
    23	endurance (speed-resisted) drills were a large contributor; and anaerobic glycolytic (AnG)
    24	work appeared **once**, in a 200m stepwise all-out time trial. Issurin's three stated
    25	takeaways: (a) even for a prominent sprinter, aerobic-endurance volume is very high in this
    26	microcycle; (b) strength can be developed effectively through force accentuation inside
    27	sport-specific drills rather than only in the weight room; (c) despite 100m Freestyle's high
    28	metabolic reliance on anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity, glycolytic *training* volume in
    29	this aerobic microcycle is negligible, reserved instead for the anaerobic microcycle (see
    30	[[framework--anaerobic-glycolytic-microcycle-design]]). Table 3.2 (PDF p. 95, printed p. 84)
    31	lists the compatible secondary modalities for an aerobic microcycle: maximum strength (first
    32	priority; combining aerobic and strength work "ensures better oxidation in enlarged
    33	muscles"), anaerobic alactic/maximum speed (sprints "break monotony and activate a wide
    34	spectrum of muscle fibers... exploited in subsequent aerobic workloads"), aerobic
    35	strength-endurance (speed-resisted exercises), and movement technique (drilled during
    36	prolonged aerobic work without aggravating metabolic adaptation). Issurin adds a specific
    37	timing rule: strength work should not follow directly after exhaustive aerobic training,
    38	because the testosterone/cortisol ratio needed for protein synthesis stays depressed for
    39	"many hours" post-endurance-work (Viru, Karelson & Smirnova, 1992); **24 hours** of recovery,
    40	with only low-level loads in between, is stated as the needed gap (PDF p. 95, printed p. 84,
    41	citing Chesley et al., 1992 for protein-turnover persisting ≥24 hours post-resistance-work).
    42	
    43	**Why it works** — Issurin's own stated mechanism for combining aerobic and strength work is
    44	that concurrent aerobic stimulus improves oxidative support in the muscle mass strength
    45	training builds, addressing the problem (raised in Chapter 1's swimmer interference case,
    46	[[case-study--concurrent-training-interference-and-decay]]) that strength-built muscle mass
    47	without matched aerobic enzyme/mitochondrial development doesn't help endurance-sport
    48	performance. The 24-hour strength-after-aerobic sequencing rule follows directly from the
    49	testosterone/cortisol citation: an anabolic hormonal environment is a precondition for the
    50	strength stimulus to "take," and that environment is temporarily suppressed right after
    51	exhaustive endurance work.
    52	
    53	**When to apply** — Designing an aerobic-base microcycle (early accumulation mesocycle, see
    54	[[framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]]) for any athlete needing both an
    55	aerobic base and strength, and specifically the 24-hour strength-after-aerobic spacing rule
    56	whenever a hard conditioning session and a strength session are close together in the same
    57	microcycle. **Inference:** for football specifically, this example argues against treating
    58	"conditioning day" and "lift day" as interchangeable slots without checking the sequencing
    59	gap, particularly early in an off-season aerobic-base block.
    60	
    61	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a single elite swimmer's program, reported
    62	secondhand by his personal coach with no comparison data and no other athletes' programs
    63	shown; it is Issurin's chosen illustrative anecdote, not a study. **Inference:** swimming's
    64	metabolic and technical demands (continuous, cyclical, non-contact, highly technique-limited)
    65	differ substantially from football; the specific finding that glycolytic training is nearly
    66	absent in this microcycle should not be read as "football conditioning should minimize
    67	glycolytic work"; Eric's baseline's own stated fall-camp priority stack treats glycolytic
    68	conditioning as something to "absorb incidentally through camp and practice" rather than
    69	program directly (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing
    70	`class-4-2026.md` pp.34, 39), which is a different reason (practical prioritization under a
    71	tight camp calendar) than Popov's reason (protecting a compatible-modality structure within
    72	one microcycle type). The 24-hour strength-after-aerobic figure rests on two cited studies
    73	(Viru et al. 1992; Chesley et al. 1992) not detailed further in this text: treat the
    74	direction as supported but the exact "24 hours" as an applied rule of thumb, not a
    75	precisely-dosed threshold verified here.
    76	
    77	**Example** — A Baylor off-season aerobic-base week could sequence a hard aerobic-threshold
    78	run or bike session on Monday, hold Tuesday's strength session to low-intensity technique
    79	work only, and place the next true max-strength session on Wednesday (at least 24 hours after
    80	Monday's endurance work, per the cited protein-turnover window), rather than programming a
    81	hard conditioning session the evening before a heavy squat day.
    82	
    83	**Related** — [[framework--anaerobic-glycolytic-microcycle-design]],
    84	[[case-study--concurrent-training-interference-and-decay]],
    85	[[framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]],
    86	[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].

    14	# The Anaerobic Glycolytic Microcycle Trades Restoration for Fatigue-Tolerant, Lactate-Driven Development
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Issurin describes the microcycle that forms the content of the transmutation
    17	mesocycle (PDF pp. 97-100, printed pp. 86-89, Table 3.3 and Figure 3.5). Its compatible
    18	modalities (Table 3.3): **strength endurance** (mostly anaerobic; high-resistance drills
    19	inside regular workouts or separate sessions; produces a dual strength-endurance and
    20	anaerobic-metabolism effect), **anaerobic alactic/maximal speed** (used by moderately fatigued
    21	athletes since a well-restored state is usually unavailable here; sprints add diversity and
    22	short-duration power contribution), **low-intensity aerobic exercise** (used throughout as
    23	active restoration, alongside stretching/relaxation), and **movement technique/tactics** (given
    24	prime placement and treated as essential despite metabolic fatigue, because competition itself
    25	imposes comparable fatigue on technique). Issurin gives specific lactate-based intensity
    26	zones: workloads producing **5-8 mM** blood lactate improve maximal aerobic power and
    27	aerobic-anaerobic interaction and are more typical early-to-mid-season; workloads above
    28	**8 mM** target anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity specifically and dominate in the final
    29	weeks before the target competition (PDF pp. 97-98, printed pp. 86-87). The worked ten-workout
    30	chart (Figure 3.5, PDF p. 100, printed p. 89) uses a three-peak load design with six
    31	development workouts (three of them key-workouts) targeting anaerobic glycolytic power,
    32	anaerobic glycolytic capacity, and strength endurance, buffered by a mid-week restoration
    33	"window" (Wednesday evening) and two medium-load alactic-maintenance sessions.
    34	
    35	**Why it works** — Issurin states the defining feature of this microcycle is fatigue
    36	accumulation with insufficient restoration by design (PDF p. 99, printed p. 88): high-load
    37	glycolytic work drives maximal heart rate/cardiac output, maximal oxygen deficit/debt and
    38	blood lactate accumulation, plus a rise in catecholamines and cortisol with testosterone
    39	suppressed for 24+ hours (citing Viru, 1995). At a workout frequency of 6-12 sessions/week,
    40	fatigue accumulation across the microcycle is "inevitable": the design goal is to manage that
    41	fatigue (through workout sequencing, deliberately-placed restoration, and monitoring) rather
    42	than to avoid it, which is what distinguishes this microcycle from the aerobic one.
    43	
    44	**When to apply** — Structuring the highest-intensity block of a transmutation mesocycle
    45	(see [[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]) when the
    46	targeted abilities are anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity and anaerobic-component strength
    47	endurance. Issurin's four stated guidelines for managing the built-in fatigue (PDF p. 99,
    48	printed p. 88): sequence development workouts with expected fatigue accumulation in mind;
    49	treat restoration workouts as a planned, non-optional part of the week; use active
    50	restoration means (stretching, low-intensity drills, massage, physiotherapy, nutritional
    51	support); and prioritize training-response monitoring here specifically. **Inference:** this
    52	maps to the hardest week(s) of fall camp or a mid-season "gut check" conditioning emphasis,
    53	where the department accepts several days of accumulating fatigue in exchange for a
    54	concentrated glycolytic-capacity stimulus, rather than trying to keep every day fresh.
    55	
    56	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The specific lactate cut-points (5-8 mM vs. >8 mM) and
    57	the 6-12 workouts/week frequency figure are presented without a cited validation study in this
    58	passage; treat them as Issurin's own applied heuristics. **Inference:** none of this section's
    59	evidence is football-specific: it is framed around individual/dual sports and combat sports
    60	with a season structure that tolerates a dedicated multi-day high-fatigue block, which is
    61	harder to fit inside a single football in-season week (see
    62	[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] for the team-sport-adapted version).
    63	**Eric's baseline** explicitly treats glycolytic conditioning for football as something to
    64	absorb incidentally through camp and practice rather than as a primary programmed target
    65	(`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` pp.34, 39),
    66	a different posture than this microcycle's deliberate, concentrated glycolytic emphasis,
    67	which is drawn from individual/dual/combat-sport programming. Blood lactate testing
    68	capability (needed to hit the stated mM zones precisely) is not a standard part of the
    69	department's documented testing stack per this baseline corpus.
    70	
    71	**Example** — A transmutation-mesocycle week built for a combat-sport or team-sport athlete
    72	needing anaerobic capacity could place three key-workouts across the week (per Figure 3.5's
    73	pattern, one each for anaerobic glycolytic power, anaerobic glycolytic capacity, and strength
    74	endurance), buffered by an alactic-maintenance session, a mid-week restoration window, and
    75	sessions blending anaerobic glycolytic power with strength endurance, accepting that athletes
    76	will not be fully restored entering most of these sessions.
    77	
    78	**Related** — [[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]],
    79	[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]],
    80	[[case-study--popov-aerobic-strength-microcycle]],
    81	[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].

    13	
    14	# Sedykh's Hammer-Throw Microcycle Puts Explosive Strength Only in Morning, Fresh-Athlete Sessions
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Issurin presents the eleven-workout microcycle of two-time Olympic champion
    17	hammer thrower Yuri Sedykh (USSR), as reported by his coach (Bondarchuk, 1986) (PDF pp.
    18	101-103, printed pp. 90-92, Table 3.4 and Figure 3.6). Four essential features: (a)
    19	event-specific explosive-strength exercises (throwing different-weight hammers), the
    20	top-priority target, appear **exclusively** in morning sessions and always in the **initial**
    21	part of the workout, to use the athlete's most favorable physical state for the key-exercise;
    22	(b) maximum-strength exercises (barbell snatch, half squats, good mornings), a supporting
    23	role, are placed in five sessions: four separate evening sessions plus once in the second
    24	part of a morning session; (c) additional explosive-strength work (standing jumps) appears
    25	three times, but never when the athlete is in his best condition, i.e., placed after the
    26	primary explosive work is already done; (d) restorative activity (basketball, swimming,
    27	stretching) is built into the program, including on the day off. Issurin separately cites a
    28	related mechanism study: Cardinale and Stone (2006) measured resting blood testosterone and
    29	countermovement vertical jump in 70 elite athletes (48 men, 22 women; sprinters, handball,
    30	volleyball, soccer) after a 10-hour fast and a rest day, finding a significant positive
    31	relationship between testosterone and jump height (r = 0.61, p < 0.001) (PDF p. 103, printed
    32	p. 92). Issurin's own stated implications from that study: athletes with relatively high
    33	testosterone (either sex) have some inherited predisposition for explosive-strength
    34	performance, and microcycle design for explosive-strength development should avoid excessive
    35	fatigue, because fatigue suppresses testosterone and sharply reduces the training effect of
    36	maximal-power exercises.
    37	
    38	**Why it works** — Issurin's stated mechanism (PDF pp. 103-104, printed pp. 92-93) is that
    39	explosive strength depends on the sensitivity
    40	and reactivity of the neuromuscular system, and excessive fatigue "disrupts the subtle
    41	regulation of neural input and muscle contraction"; testosterone is named as the hormone
    42	determining strength training's anabolic effect and as an index of induced physical stress
    43	(Viru and Viru, 2000). **Inference:** the placement rule (explosive work only when fresh,
    44	morning, first in the session) follows directly from this same logic already generalized in
    45	[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]]: CNS-dependent, high-precision qualities
    46	need a well-rested athlete, and this case study is simply that general rule applied to one
    47	specific, historically documented program.
    48	
    49	**When to apply** — As a concrete illustration of sequencing explosive/technical power work
    50	at the very start of a session, before any fatigue-inducing supporting work, for athletes
    51	whose primary target ability is explosive strength in a highly coordinated skill.
    52	**Inference:** in football, this maps most directly to skill-position or specialist
    53	explosive-power development (e.g., jump-training or Olympic-lift-variant work meant to
    54	transfer to explosive movement): placing that work first in a session, before conditioning
    55	or high-volume accessory work, mirrors Sedykh's morning-first placement of hammer throws.
    56	
    57	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a single elite thrower's program from a single
    58	coach's secondhand report (Bondarchuk, 1986), with no comparison athlete or outcome data
    59	beyond the general BPC narrative already logged in
    60	[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]]: it illustrates a design principle,
    61	not a validated dose-response result. **Inference:** hammer throw is an acyclic, single-effort,
    62	highly technical power event with no contact and no in-competition fatigue accumulation across
    63	a "game," unlike football; the specific workout counts, throw counts, and session splits in
    64	Table 3.4 should not be copied as a template. The testosterone-jump correlation (Cardinale and
    65	Stone, 2006) is cross-sectional and observational (r = 0.61 explains well under half the
    66	variance in jump height): it identifies an association at one time point in rested athletes,
    67	not a training intervention; it does not establish that raising testosterone directly causes
    68	higher jump performance, only that they covary. Population also spans track, handball,
    69	volleyball and soccer athletes of both sexes, not football specifically.
    70	
    71	**Example** — A football skill player's Tuesday lift built around explosive-power development
    72	(e.g., trap-bar jumps, medicine-ball throws) should be sequenced first in the session, on a day
    73	following adequate rest, with any high-volume or fatiguing accessory work placed afterward,
    74	not the reverse.
    75	
    76	**Related** — [[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
    77	[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]],
    78	[[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]].

    13	
    14	# Six Microcycle Types by Purpose and Load, With One-, Two-, and Three-Peak Weekly Load Waves
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Table 3.1 (PDF p. 88, printed p. 77; verified against the page image)
    17	gives six microcycle types, each with a stated purpose, load level, design particular, and
    18	duration range: **Adjustment** (initial adaptation to loads, medium load, gradual workload
    19	increase, **5-7 days**); **Loading** (fitness development, substantial-high load, big/substantial
    20	workloads, **5-9 days**); **Impact** (fitness development via extreme stimuli, very
    21	high-extreme load, summation of extreme workloads, **4-7 days**); **Pre-competitive**
    22	(immediate preparation for competition, medium load, tuning with event-specific means,
    23	**5-7 days**, see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] for full detail);
    24	**Competitive** (participation in competition, high-very high load, sport/event-specific
    25	performance, **2-7 days**); **Restoration** (active recovery, low load, wide spectrum of
    26	restorative means, **3-7 days**). Issurin notes the adjustment microcycle can shorten to
    27	3-5 days mid-season (e.g., starting a new training stage or a camp), and the restoration
    28	microcycle after camp or competition typically runs 3-4 days mid-season (PDF p. 88, printed
    29	p. 77). Separately, Issurin describes load variation **within** a microcycle as a "wave-shape
    30	design" using the 5-point load scale from [[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]]:
    31	Figure 3.1 (PDF p. 90, printed p. 79) shows one-, two-, and three-peak weekly load patterns
    32	for single-workout-per-day microcycles. Two- and three-peak designs are described as "used
    33	most widely" because they let athletes handle a relatively large weekly workload with reduced
    34	excessive-fatigue risk; the one-peak design concentrates several developmental workouts for a
    35	"more profound and stressful training response," a pattern reserved for "sufficiently
    36	prepared high-performance athletes" and not for novices. For microcycles with two workouts
    37	per day, Figure 3.2 (PDF p. 91, printed p. 80) gives a worked ten-workout example: two
    38	development workouts open the week (first peak), two medium-load supporting workouts
    39	provide restoration, then a three-session mini-block including two key-workouts forms the
    40	second peak, with the week's final session usable as a time-trial or scrimmage.
    41	
    42	**Why it works** — Issurin frames the point-scale quantification (adapted from the 5-point
    43	load scale) as serving three purposes: it lets coaches in non-measurable sports (sailing,
    44	team/dual sports) express load numerically and visually; it lets athletes see and
    45	consciously anticipate key-workouts and the restoration that follows load peaks
    46	(a didactic use); and it lets whole microcycles be compared to each other for planning
    47	purposes (PDF pp. 91-92, printed pp. 80-81). The peak/trough pattern itself follows the same
    48	general logic as [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]: concentrating the
    49	week's hardest sessions into one, two, or three peaks (rather than spreading maximal effort
    50	evenly across every day) lets fatigue clear between peaks so each peak can still be
    51	performed at a high standard.
    52	
    53	**When to apply** — Classifying a week's purpose before assigning workouts to it (is this
    54	week meant to adjust athletes to new load, develop fitness, deliver an extreme stimulus, tune
    55	for competition, compete, or actively recover), and then shaping that week's daily load curve
    56	around one, two, or three peaks depending on athlete level and the week's targeted abilities.
    57	**Inference, mapped to a college football calendar:** early fall camp days function like
    58	Issurin's **adjustment** microcycle (medium load, gradual ramp, until two-a-days are
    59	tolerated); the heaviest camp week(s) resemble the **impact** type (very high-extreme load,
    60	short duration, 4-7 days, matching the "impact week" concept sometimes used informally in
    61	strength-staff planning); the week of the season opener and each bowl-prep week function as
    62	**pre-competitive** microcycles (see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]]); a
    63	normal in-season game week is Issurin's **competitive** microcycle in form (the whole week
    64	organized around one **competition**, 2-7 days), though its internal training content is
    65	closer to what [[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] describes; and a bye
    66	week or the week after a game before a short turnaround functions as a **restoration**
    67	microcycle. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name these six categories explicitly, but
    68	the general planning language ("a 'training week' does not have to equal 7 calendar days,"
    69	`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing week1-lecture.md p.39) is
    70	consistent with treating microcycle type, not just calendar week, as the planning unit.
    71	
    72	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The six-type table's specific duration ranges are
    73	Issurin's own applied categorization; no citation or derivation is given for why, e.g., the
    74	loading type is 5-9 days rather than some other range. **Inference:** none of the six types
    75	or the one-/two-/three-peak wave figures are demonstrated on a team-sport example in this
    76	section (that comes later, 3.1.7); the load-wave figures here are drawn from individual/dual
    77	sport contexts, and the specific number-of-peaks guidance ("one-peak... not [for] novice and
    78	less prepared athletes") is stated for individual-sport training loads, not validated for a
    79	100+ player roster with heterogeneous training ages. The point-scale system inherits every
    80	limitation already logged for the underlying RPE/restoration-time scale in
    81	[[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]] (subjective, no cited validation
    82	of the specific cut-points).
    83	
    84	**Example** — A four-week fall-camp block could be read as adjustment (days 1-5, single
    85	practices, medium load) into loading (days 6-14, one-a-days plus early two-a-days) into an
    86	impact microcycle (the hardest stretch of two-a-days, 4-7 days) into a pre-competitive
    87	microcycle in the week before the opener, each transition marked by a deliberate change in
    88	purpose and load level, not just a generic "camp is getting harder" narrative.
    89	
    90	**Related** — [[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]] (the 5-point scale
    91	this section's point-quantification is built on), [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]],
    92	[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]],
    93	[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]],
    94	[[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]].

    13	
    14	# Popov's Aerobic Microcycle: Anaerobic Glycolytic Work Is Nearly Absent Even for a 100m Freestyle Sprinter
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Issurin presents Alexander Popov's (Russia, multi-Olympic/World 50-100m
    17	Freestyle swimming champion) typical strength-aerobic microcycle from his preparatory phase
    18	(the accumulation mesocycle, in Block Periodization terms) as an example (PDF pp. 92-94,
    19	printed pp. 81-83, Figure 3.3 and Table 3.2; sourced to "courtesy of Gennadi Touretski,
    20	personal communication," Popov's coach). Across ten workouts, anaerobic threshold (AT) work
    21	and technical stroke-count drills dominated; maximal-speed (alactic) exercises appeared daily
    22	in medium proportions; aerobic power (AP) work appeared in only three workouts; strength
    23	endurance (speed-resisted) drills were a large contributor; and anaerobic glycolytic (AnG)
    24	work appeared **once**, in a 200m stepwise all-out time trial. Issurin's three stated
    25	takeaways: (a) even for a prominent sprinter, aerobic-endurance volume is very high in this
    26	microcycle; (b) strength can be developed effectively through force accentuation inside
    27	sport-specific drills rather than only in the weight room; (c) despite 100m Freestyle's high
    28	metabolic reliance on anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity, glycolytic *training* volume in
    29	this aerobic microcycle is negligible, reserved instead for the anaerobic microcycle (see
    30	[[framework--anaerobic-glycolytic-microcycle-design]]). Table 3.2 (PDF p. 95, printed p. 84)
    31	lists the compatible secondary modalities for an aerobic microcycle: maximum strength (first
    32	priority; combining aerobic and strength work "ensures better oxidation in enlarged
    33	muscles"), anaerobic alactic/maximum speed (sprints "break monotony and activate a wide
    34	spectrum of muscle fibers... exploited in subsequent aerobic workloads"), aerobic
    35	strength-endurance (speed-resisted exercises), and movement technique (drilled during
    36	prolonged aerobic work without aggravating metabolic adaptation). Issurin adds a specific
    37	timing rule: strength work should not follow directly after exhaustive aerobic training,
    38	because the testosterone/cortisol ratio needed for protein synthesis stays depressed for
    39	"many hours" post-endurance-work (Viru, Karelson & Smirnova, 1992); **24 hours** of recovery,
    40	with only low-level loads in between, is stated as the needed gap (PDF p. 95, printed p. 84,
    41	citing Chesley et al., 1992 for protein-turnover persisting ≥24 hours post-resistance-work).
    42	
    43	**Why it works** — Issurin's own stated mechanism for combining aerobic and strength work is
    44	that concurrent aerobic stimulus improves oxidative support in the muscle mass strength
    45	training builds, addressing the problem (raised in Chapter 1's swimmer interference case,
    46	[[case-study--concurrent-training-interference-and-decay]]) that strength-built muscle mass
    47	without matched aerobic enzyme/mitochondrial development doesn't help endurance-sport
    48	performance. The 24-hour strength-after-aerobic sequencing rule follows directly from the
    49	testosterone/cortisol citation: an anabolic hormonal environment is a precondition for the
    50	strength stimulus to "take," and that environment is temporarily suppressed right after
    51	exhaustive endurance work.
    52	
    53	**When to apply** — Designing an aerobic-base microcycle (early accumulation mesocycle, see
    54	[[framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]]) for any athlete needing both an
    55	aerobic base and strength, and specifically the 24-hour strength-after-aerobic spacing rule
    56	whenever a hard conditioning session and a strength session are close together in the same
    57	microcycle. **Inference:** for football specifically, this example argues against treating
    58	"conditioning day" and "lift day" as interchangeable slots without checking the sequencing
    59	gap, particularly early in an off-season aerobic-base block.
    60	
    61	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a single elite swimmer's program, reported
    62	secondhand by his personal coach with no comparison data and no other athletes' programs
    63	shown; it is Issurin's chosen illustrative anecdote, not a study. **Inference:** swimming's
    64	metabolic and technical demands (continuous, cyclical, non-contact, highly technique-limited)
    65	differ substantially from football; the specific finding that glycolytic training is nearly
    66	absent in this microcycle should not be read as "football conditioning should minimize
    67	glycolytic work"; Eric's baseline's own stated fall-camp priority stack treats glycolytic
    68	conditioning as something to "absorb incidentally through camp and practice" rather than
    69	program directly (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing
    70	`class-4-2026.md` pp.34, 39), which is a different reason (practical prioritization under a
    71	tight camp calendar) than Popov's reason (protecting a compatible-modality structure within
    72	one microcycle type). The 24-hour strength-after-aerobic figure rests on two cited studies
    73	(Viru et al. 1992; Chesley et al. 1992) not detailed further in this text: treat the
    74	direction as supported but the exact "24 hours" as an applied rule of thumb, not a
    75	precisely-dosed threshold verified here.
    76	
    77	**Example** — A Baylor off-season aerobic-base week could sequence a hard aerobic-threshold
    78	run or bike session on Monday, hold Tuesday's strength session to low-intensity technique
    79	work only, and place the next true max-strength session on Wednesday (at least 24 hours after
    80	Monday's endurance work, per the cited protein-turnover window), rather than programming a
    81	hard conditioning session the evening before a heavy squat day.
    82	
    83	**Related** — [[framework--anaerobic-glycolytic-microcycle-design]],
    84	[[case-study--concurrent-training-interference-and-decay]],
    85	[[framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]],
    86	[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].

    40	fatigue accumulation across the microcycle is "inevitable": the design goal is to manage that
    41	fatigue (through workout sequencing, deliberately-placed restoration, and monitoring) rather
    42	than to avoid it, which is what distinguishes this microcycle from the aerobic one.
    43	
    44	**When to apply** — Structuring the highest-intensity block of a transmutation mesocycle
    45	(see [[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]) when the
    46	targeted abilities are anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity and anaerobic-component strength
    47	endurance. Issurin's four stated guidelines for managing the built-in fatigue (PDF p. 99,
    48	printed p. 88): sequence development workouts with expected fatigue accumulation in mind;
    49	treat restoration workouts as a planned, non-optional part of the week; use active
    50	restoration means (stretching, low-intensity drills, massage, physiotherapy, nutritional
    51	support); and prioritize training-response monitoring here specifically. **Inference:** this
    52	maps to the hardest week(s) of fall camp or a mid-season "gut check" conditioning emphasis,

    54	concentrated glycolytic-capacity stimulus, rather than trying to keep every day fresh.

    57	the 6-12 workouts/week frequency figure are presented without a cited validation study in this
    58	passage; treat them as Issurin's own applied heuristics. **Inference:** none of this section's

    20	top-priority target, appear **exclusively** in morning sessions and always in the **initial**
    21	part of the workout, to use the athlete's most favorable physical state for the key-exercise;
    22	(b) maximum-strength exercises (barbell snatch, half squats, good mornings), a supporting
    23	role, are placed in five sessions: four separate evening sessions plus once in the second
    24	part of a morning session; (c) additional explosive-strength work (standing jumps) appears
    25	three times, but never when the athlete is in his best condition, i.e., placed after the
    26	primary explosive work is already done; (d) restorative activity (basketball, swimming,
    27	stretching) is built into the program, including on the day off. Issurin separately cites a
    28	related mechanism study: Cardinale and Stone (2006) measured resting blood testosterone and
    29	countermovement vertical jump in 70 elite athletes (48 men, 22 women; sprinters, handball,
    30	volleyball, soccer) after a 10-hour fast and a rest day, finding a significant positive
    31	relationship between testosterone and jump height (r = 0.61, p < 0.001) (PDF p. 103, printed
    32	p. 92). Issurin's own stated implications from that study: athletes with relatively high
    33	testosterone (either sex) have some inherited predisposition for explosive-strength
    34	performance, and microcycle design for explosive-strength development should avoid excessive
    35	fatigue, because fatigue suppresses testosterone and sharply reduces the training effect of
    36	maximal-power exercises.
    37	
    38	**Why it works** — Issurin's stated mechanism (PDF pp. 103-104, printed pp. 92-93) is that
    39	explosive strength depends on the sensitivity
    40	and reactivity of the neuromuscular system, and excessive fatigue "disrupts the subtle
    41	regulation of neural input and muscle contraction"; testosterone is named as the hormone
    42	determining strength training's anabolic effect and as an index of induced physical stress
    43	(Viru and Viru, 2000). **Inference:** the placement rule (explosive work only when fresh,
    44	morning, first in the session) follows directly from this same logic already generalized in
    45	[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]]: CNS-dependent, high-precision qualities
    46	need a well-rested athlete, and this case study is simply that general rule applied to one
    47	specific, historically documented program.

    50	at the very start of a session, before any fatigue-inducing supporting work, for athletes
    51	whose primary target ability is explosive strength in a highly coordinated skill.

    55	or high-volume accessory work, mirrors Sedykh's morning-first placement of hammer throws.

    14	# The Pre-Competitive Microcycle: Cut Volume Hard, Raise Maximal-Speed and Sport-Specific Work, Keep Frequency
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The pre-competitive microcycle forms the content of the realization
    17	mesocycle (see [[framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]]) and is also called the
    18	taper at the microcycle level (PDF pp. 104-105, printed pp. 93-94; verified against page
    19	images). It must satisfy three demands (PDF p. 104, printed p. 93): sport-specific
    20	exercises/tasks that simulate the forthcoming competition and build mental readiness and
    21	toughness; development of maximal speed/power and sport-specific quickness; and full (or
    22	partial) restoration after the preceding transmutation mesocycle's fatiguing workloads. Table
    23	3.5 (PDF p. 105, printed p. 94, verified against page image) gives seven prescriptive
    24	characteristics: **workload volume**, substantially reduced, to create conditions for full
    25	recovery; **volume of intense exercises specifically**, substantially reduced versus the
    26	prior mesocycle, so total drill volume falls but quality rises; **contribution of maximum
    27	speed/power exercises**, substantially **increased** (well-rested athletes respond better to
    28	maximal-speed drills, and maximal-speed training residuals are the shortest of any ability, per
    29	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]); **contribution of
    30	sport-specific tasks**, substantially increased (simulative tasks improve adaptation to
    31	expected competitive stressors); **workout frequency**, usually kept **similar** to the
    32	previous mesocycle (subdividing the same total work into more, smaller portions raises
    33	quality per session even as volume falls); **organization**, a rational mix of group,
    34	individual and mixed workouts, weighted somewhat more toward individual work than usual, so
    35	athletes can attend to personal technical detail and coach rapport; **restoration**,
    36	deliberately favorable conditions and an increased volume of restorative exercises/workouts,
    37	since athletes have more free time and motivation to use it. Issurin states that in qualified
    38	athletes, especially during a pre-competitive training camp, maintaining frequency in practice
    39	means **eight to ten workouts per week** even as volume per workout drops (PDF p. 106, printed
    40	p. 95). Workout timing should match the expected competition's daily biological-rhythm window
    41	(example given: Olympic canoe-kayak/rowing regattas run only in the morning, so pre-Olympic
    42	training is scheduled to place peak-effort sessions at that same morning time, PDF p. 107,
    43	printed p. 96). Figure 3.7 (PDF p. 108, printed p. 97) gives a worked chart for a
    44	morning-peak-performance pre-competitive microcycle, alternating maximum-strength/technique
    45	mornings with sport-specific-simulation/alactic afternoons, moving toward heavier
    46	sport-specific-simulation and explosive-strength content later in the week. On strength work
    47	specifically, Issurin notes a real disagreement in the field: many athletes (particularly
    48	swimmers, per Platonov & Fesenko, 1990, and also reported among volleyball and tennis players)
    49	report high-resistance work pre-competition degrades fine technical skill, arguing for
    50	reducing or excluding it; but sport-specific maximal/explosive strength work is also argued to
    51	maintain the technical force component (Bompa & Carrera, 2003) and to prevent uncontrolled,
    52	stress-hormone-driven muscle-mass loss pre-competition (PDF p. 108, printed p. 97).

    54	**Why it works** — Reduced total load is stated as the "principal condition" for reaching
    55	supercompensation before competition (PDF p. 106, printed p. 95); the two things this

    58	energy-resource availability (maximal speed) or on the athlete's capacity to fully attend to
    59	technical/tactical detail under simulated competitive stress (sport-specific tasks). Keeping
    60	frequency similar while cutting volume is explicitly a quality lever, not a rest lever: more,
    61	shorter, higher-quality sessions rather than fewer long ones.

    64	week(s) immediately before a bowl game map most directly onto this framework: cut total

    72	adaptation Issurin gives later in this chapter. **Season opener after fall camp:** the final

    74	volume should come down from camp peak even though frequency (practice count) may stay similar.

    97	"8-10 workouts per week" frequency figure assumes an individual/dual-sport training camp

    99	week. Issurin does not address game-week travel, opponent scouting load, or academic-calendar

   103	while cutting total practice/lift volume substantially, shifting a larger share of practice
   104	time to explosive/speed work and full-speed game-plan simulation than a mid-season week would
   105	carry, and deliberately expanding individual position-group time (film, technique correction)
   106	relative to full-team periods, while treating the "how much to lift" question as an open

    14	# A Two-Mini-Block Weekly Structure for In-Season Team Sports, Naming American Football Directly
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Issurin addresses the specific constraint that team and dual sports (he
    17	names **soccer, American football, rugby, volleyball** explicitly) run a 20-35 week season
    18	where "the possibility of inserting highly concentrated training blocks is very limited"
    19	(PDF pp. 108-109, printed pp. 97-98). He cites Fleck and Kraemer (1997): players typically
    20	maintain strength near pre-season levels for 14-16 weeks, after which strength variables
    21	decrease dramatically. Because the usual one-week gap between games is too short to work
    22	effectively on every training target (metabolic conditioning, maximal/explosive strength,
    23	injury prevention, techno-tactical skill, game-specific endurance, active restoration) at once,
    24	Issurin proposes adapting three BPC approaches at the *week* level: high concentration of
    25	specialized workloads within **mini-blocks**, separating mini-blocks by training modality, and
    26	determining **key-workouts** within each mini-block. The worked example (Figure 3.8, PDF p.
    27	109, printed p. 98, "based on Baker, 2001," a real cited source, not an uncited synthesis)
    28	splits a standard Monday-Sunday week into two mini-blocks. **Mini-block 1 (Monday-Wednesday)**
    29	targets sport-specific maximal and explosive strength as the dominant training aim: it opens
    30	Monday with an active-recovery session (medium/low load, aerobic and general conditioning),
    31	then delivers the strength emphasis across **two key-workouts**, combined with a medium-load
    32	team practice (Tuesday afternoon) and a conditioning-restorative workout (Wednesday afternoon).
    33	This sequencing leaves **28-30 hours of recovery** after the strength key-workouts before
    34	mini-block 2 begins, to let the anabolic/restorative process run before the next demand.
    35	**Mini-block 2 (Thursday-Saturday)** targets sport-specific team practice and immediate game
    36	preparation: it includes two obligatory team practices, one before the day off (intended to
    37	deliver a pronounced game-specific stimulus) and a second, load-restricted session immediately
    38	before the game itself (mostly techno-tactical drills tied to the specific forthcoming
    39	opponent). Issurin notes some highly motivated teams skip the day off and add an optional
    40	Friday-morning conditioning or techno-tactical session instead, trading recovery time for
    41	extra preparation; he states the tradeoff explicitly without endorsing either choice. The
    42	chart gives priority to maximal-strength development over explosive-type work within the week,
    43	which Issurin explains as protecting "somatic, functional and anabolic status," while noting a
    44	cited counter-example (Newton et al., 2006) of sequencing classic high-resistance training with
    45	ballistic explosive-type mesocycles to enhance jump performance instead.
    46	
    47	**Why it works** — The mini-block structure is this chapter's direct answer to the constraint
    48	stated in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (BPC needs concentrated,
    49	sequenced blocks) meeting the constraint that team sports cannot suspend competition long
    50	enough to run full-length accumulation/transmutation/realization mesocycles
    51	(see [[framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]] and
    52	[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]] for what those
    53	normally require in duration). Splitting the week itself into two purpose-specific mini-blocks,
    54	each with its own key-workouts, is Issurin's way of keeping some of BPC's concentration
    55	benefit even though the underlying block can only be one week long, not several.
    56

    58	strength-and-conditioning miss-log's "peaking phase structure for collegiate football" gap
    59	(logged 2026-09-03)** — Issurin explicitly names American football as a sport this structure
    60	is meant for. **Eric's baseline's** in-season rule, "maintain intensity, reduce volume"
    61	(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md`
    62	pp.20-21), is compatible with and gets a concrete weekly shape from this framework: the
    63	early-week mini-block is where intensity (maximal/explosive strength) gets its two key-workouts,
    64	while the late-week mini-block is deliberately techno-tactical and load-restricted heading into
    65	the game, which *is* the volume reduction the baseline rule calls for. The 28-30 hour recovery
    66	window between the strength mini-block and the practice-heavy mini-block gives a specific,
    67	citable number for how much gap a college program might target between its heaviest in-season
    68	lift and the next high-intensity team session.
    69	
    70	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The specific day-by-day chart (Figure 3.8) is built from
    71	one cited source, Baker (2001), a study of professional and college-aged rugby league players'
    72	in-season concurrent training: a real, checkable citation, but a single study in rugby league,
    73	a sport with a different weekly game/practice rhythm than college football, which layers

    17	microcycle (Table 3.6, PDF p. 111, printed p. 100): (1) determine dominant and secondary
    18	training modalities, based on the annual plan and the current mesocycle's specificity; (2)
    19	determine, place and compile **key-workouts** (see

    21	impact; (3) determine restorative workouts and restorative "windows," to facilitate the
    22	key-workouts and prevent excess fatigue; (4) determine, place and compile other
    23	developmental/supportive workouts, paying special attention to how preceding workouts affect
    24	sensitivity to subsequent ones; (5) select monitoring means for the targeted abilities and
    25	functions; (6) plan special events (psychologist, physician, team meeting, etc.). Alongside
    26	this sequence, Issurin states five general design rules (PDF p. 112, printed p. 101):
    27	**first**, key-workout priority: once targeted abilities are defined, design should
    28	start from the key-workouts, not fill them in last; **second**, arrangement around
    29	key-workouts: the preceding session affects the athlete's sensitivity to the key-workout's
    30	stimulus, while the following session determines fatigue accumulation and restoration, so both
    31	neighbors must be chosen deliberately; **third**, sharing restorative means: restorative
    32	workouts, restorative exercises (low-intensity aerobic work, stretching, relaxation, shaking,
    33	breathing) and restorative procedures (massage, sauna, hydro/physiotherapy, mental training)
    34	are "indispensable" and must be expertly planned into every microcycle, not treated as
    35	optional filler; **fourth**, workload initiation and peaks: a day off lowers readiness for
    36	high workloads, so the first session after a day off should **not** be a key-workout; the
    37	number and placement of key-workouts is what determines whether the week is a one-, two-, or
    38	three-peak design (see [[framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]]); **fifth**,
    39	monitoring: key-workout execution data (achievement level, technical quality, HR, blood
    40	lactate, RPE) is the single best indicator of an athlete's current state.
    41	
    42	**Why it works** — This is a process heuristic, not a physiological mechanism: Issurin's
    43	stated rationale is that once the microcycle's actual development stimulus (the key-workouts)
    44	is fixed, every other design decision (what precedes it, what follows it, how restoration is
    45	distributed) exists to protect that stimulus's quality and manage the fatigue it produces.
    46	Designing "everything else first, then slotting in the hard part" risks the key-workout landing
    47	on a fatigued or under-prepared athlete.
    48	
    49	**When to apply** — As a checklist when building or auditing any microcycle: has the dominant
    50	modality been named before workouts were scheduled; are the key-workouts placed away from the
    51	first session after a day off; is there a planned restorative window around each key-workout;
    52	and is monitoring tied specifically to key-workout performance rather than spread evenly across
    53	every session. Useful as a coach-facing planning template independent of sport.
    54	
    55	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is Issurin's own applied synthesis of BPC design
    56	logic; no citation or comparative study is given for the six-step sequence or the five rules
    57	themselves. Treat them as a structured practitioner heuristic, not an experimentally
    58	validated planning method. **Inference:** the sequence assumes a coach already has a clear
    59	single dominant-and-secondary modality assignment for the week (step 1); it gives no guidance
    60	for a team-sport week that must simultaneously serve several position groups with different
    61	dominant needs on the same day, a common real constraint in football that this chapter's
    62	narrower single-athlete/single-event examples elsewhere do not have to solve.
    63	
    64	**Example** — Before finalizing a week's training plan, a coach could walk the six steps in
    65	order: name this week's dominant ability, place its key-workouts (never as the first session
    66	after a day off), build restorative windows around them, fill in supporting sessions with an
    67	eye to how each affects the next, pick 2-3 monitoring indicators tied to the key-workouts, and
    68	only then schedule any non-training events.
    69	
    70	**Related** — [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]],
    71	[[framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]],
    72	[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]].
