    60	study: **20 highly qualified male long-distance triathletes**, tracked across a 4-week
    61	high-workload mesocycle into a **2-week taper mesocycle** (PDF pp. 126-127, printed pp.

    64	change, but body fat mass **increased by 4.3%**. Issurin's point: unchanged body mass can mask
    65	a real fat gain (or muscle loss) if eating habits don't adjust downward with the drop in
    66	training energy cost, so body mass alone is "not always a reliable" anthropometric indicator
    67	during a taper.

    70	already given for the pre-competitive microcycle
    71	(see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]], which is this mesocycle's dominant
    72	microcycle type): the targeted abilities need a well-rested nervous system and available energy
    73	stores, so load must come down before those specific qualities can actually be trained and
    74	expressed. The duration-sensitivity point (too long detrains, too short under-restores) is
    75	Issurin's own applied synthesis, though he cites Mujika et al. (2004), a real, checkable
    76	taper-physiology review, as the source flagging this contradiction in the field generally,
    77	not something Issurin resolves with his own data here.
    78	
    79	**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college football calendar** — **Bowl prep** is the
    80	clearest college-football analog to a full one-to-three-week realization mesocycle: workload
    81	should come down substantially from whatever preceded it (regular-season maintenance load, or a
    82	short rebuild block if the last-game-to-bowl gap was used as a mini accumulation/transmutation
    83	sequence, see [[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]]), practice time
    84	should shift toward maximal-speed/explosive work and heavily rehearsed, opponent-specific
    85	game-plan simulation (the Table 3.13 dosage pattern, adapted from race-quarters to game-plan
    86	segments, e.g., specific down-and-distance packages, specific special-teams looks), and staff
    87	should watch emotional tension deliberately given a long layoff and a non-conference,
    88	lower-frequency opponent-preparation rhythm. **The gap between the final regular-season/
    89	conference-championship game and the bowl game** is exactly the scheduling problem Issurin's
    90	duration-sensitivity warning describes: too long a "taper-only" approach across that whole gap
    91	risks detraining (per Mujika et al., 2004, and consistent with
    92	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]'s ~30-day residual windows for
    93	basic abilities), which is the direct rationale for treating the early part of that gap as a
    94	short accumulation/transmutation rebuild and only the final 1-3 weeks before the bowl as this
    95	realization mesocycle. The nutrition warning (unchanged eating during a lower-workload window
    96	risks fat gain even at stable body mass) is directly transferable to any football taper or bowl
    97	prep window and worth flagging to Performance Nutrition specifically, since body-composition
    98	oversight sits with that separate Health & Wellness unit per Eric's baseline
    99	(`method-baseline.md`, "Nutrition and body composition"). **Eric's baseline** gives no duration

   127	either excess complacency (too little anxiety, given the layoff and often lower-stakes framing

    14	# Transmutation Mesocycle: Capped at About Four Weeks by Fatigue and by the Aerobic Residual Clock
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The transmutation mesocycle "transmutes accumulated basic abilities into
    17	specific physical and techno-tactical fitness" and is characterized by more specialized
    18	targeted abilities, higher-intensity/higher-volume developmental workloads, and being "the most
    19	fatiguing mesocycle" (PDF p. 118, printed p. 107; verified against page image). Table 3.9 gives
    20	three duration-limiting factors: **fatigue accumulation** from highly concentrated intense
    21	workloads approaches its upper limit in **3-4 weeks** (obviated by inserting a restorative
    22	microcycle or an aerobic mini-block); **the residual training effect of the preceding
    23	(accumulation) mesocycle**, since after 4 weeks of highly intense work the effect of the prior
    24	aerobic-strength mesocycle "drops dramatically," per the roughly 30-day residual windows in
    25	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]; and **the competition
    26	calendar**, which can force a shorter mesocycle regardless of the other two factors. Net rule:
    27	the transmutation mesocycle "usually lasts no more than four weeks" (PDF pp. 118-119, printed
    28	pp. 107-108). Issurin flags a real methodical contradiction here: many sports need anaerobic
    29	glycolytic development over a longer period than four weeks allows without letting the
    30	accumulation mesocycle's aerobic/strength residual decay; the stated fix is inserting a
    31	short aerobic mini-block inside the transmutation mesocycle (elaborated in
    32	[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]]). Content (Table 3.10, PDF p. 119,
    33	printed p. 108) sequences: an **initial** loading microcycle (usually one week) with gradually
    34	increasing load; **mid-and-ending** loading and/or impact microcycles (impact can run 3-4 days);
    35	and optional insertions, including a **competition/trial** microcycle (participating fatigued is
    36	not excluded; athletes tend to experience the competitive workload itself as a relative load
    37	reduction, and expect no personal best from it), a **restoration** microcycle (planned in
    38	advance or triggered individually as athletes near their adaptation limit), or a short
    39	**aerobic contrast mini-block** (2-4 days, to prolong aerobic training residuals and partly
    40	restore athletes for the next high-intensity stretch). Monitoring (Table 3.11, PDF p. 120,
    41	printed p. 109) again tracks workload performance, targeted (sport-specific) ability results,
    42	and training responses, but with an added emphasis here: **subjective self-estimation of
    43	fatigue, stress, sleep, and muscle soreness**, because "maximal workloads elicit maximal
    44	training responses" and "much confidence between the coach and athlete is very important."
    45	Because dosing near the "upper limits of adaptation" is described as the transmutation
    46	mesocycle's biggest problem, Issurin gives Peter Snell's (Olympic champion runner and sport
    47	physiologist) definition of overtraining: "a state in which performance diminishes while the
    48	level of training is maintained or increased" (Snell, 1990), and lists five early warning
    49	signals (Burke et al., 1990; Hooper et al., 1995, PDF p. 121, printed p. 110): resting HR up
    50	more than **5 beats/min over 3-5 days**; persistent or rapid body-mass decrease; persistent
    51	increased general fatigue; persistent increased muscle soreness; persistent increased sleep
    52	disturbance. A supporting case study (Hooper et al., 1995, same locator): **19 elite swimmers**
    53	monitored over 6 months with a large blood/urine/hormone/CPK/HR/blood-pressure battery plus
    54	daily self-reported stress, fatigue, sleep quality, and muscle soreness (1-7 scale); **three**
    55	swimmers were diagnosed overtrained during the study, but stale-vs-non-stale athletes did
    56	**not** differ on any blood, urine, or physiological marker at mid- or late-season. The
    57	difference showed up clearly and significantly only in the subjective fatigue/soreness
    58	ratings, and a multi-component model using those four subjective ratings predicted competitive
    59	performance changes; adding more objective indicators did not improve prediction accuracy.
    60	
    61	**Why it works** — The duration cap follows directly from stacking two decay clocks against
    62	each other: fatigue from concentrated intense work saturates in 3-4 weeks, and the prior
    63	mesocycle's basic-ability residual (aerobic endurance, max strength, ~30 days per
    64	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]) also runs out around then, so
    65	a transmutation mesocycle that runs longer risks both overtraining and arriving at competition
    66	with degraded basic abilities. The Hooper et al. (1995) finding, that cheap subjective ratings
    67	out-predicted an expensive blood/hormone panel, is presented as direct evidence that
    68	systematic self-report monitoring is not a "budget substitute" for physiological testing in
    69	this specific application; it is described as the more sensitive tool for catching overtraining
    70	in this data set.
    71	
    72	**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college football calendar** — The **middle-to-late
    73	weeks of fall camp**, where two-a-days and the highest-intensity, most sport-specific
    74	(scrimmage-heavy) work concentrate, are functionally a transmutation mesocycle and should be
    75	capped near the same 3-4 week outer limit Issurin gives, both to avoid overtraining and because
    76	any aerobic/strength base built in an early-camp or summer accumulation phase will itself decay
    77	on roughly the same clock. Any old-school "keep hammering all camp" plan without at least one
    78	built-in restorative window or aerobic mini-block runs against both duration-limiting factors
    79	here at once. **Eric's baseline** does not name Snell's overtraining definition or the
    80	five warning signs, but the department's stated preference for practical, athlete-reportable
    81	signals over burdensome batteries (`method-baseline.md`, "Load monitoring and GPS," discussing
    82	why daily wellness surveys were tried) is philosophically aligned with the Hooper et al.
    83	finding, though see the "Contested" note below: the baseline corpus's own experience is that a
    84	*specific* subjective wellness survey was later abandoned because athletes learned to game it.
    85	
    86	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — **Population caveat:** every piece of supporting evidence
    87	in this section (Sharobajko's kayakers referenced upstream, Hooper's 19 elite swimmers, Snell's
    88	own middle-distance-running background) comes from individual endurance/technical sports, not
    89	football; the 5 beats/min-over-3-5-days resting-HR threshold and the 3-4 week duration cap are
    90	Issurin's own applied synthesis with no controlled dose-response citation. **Contested: this
    91	frontmatter rating is set for the following specific conflict, not for the whole entry.** The
    92	Hooper et al. (1995) result (subjective ratings beat objective blood/hormone markers for
    93	overtraining detection) sits in direct tension with Eric's baseline's own SportSmith-documented
    94	decision to replace subjective daily wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI,
    95	specifically because "inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" and subjective
    96	self-report "couldn't be trusted" at scale (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and
    97	neuromuscular monitoring" and "Philosophy and decision principles," citing
    98	`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md` and `2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`). This is
    99	the same coach's-eye/subjective-vs-objective tension already logged in the baseline's own
   100	"Tensions and contradictions" section (#3), now sharpened by a specific study on the Issurin
   101	side of it. Do not treat either position as settled without discussing the difference in sample
   102	size (n=19 vs. a 120+ player roster), duration (6 months vs. an academic year-plus), and survey
   103	design (a validated multi-marker overtraining battery vs. a general daily wellness check); the
   104	two findings could both be true of their own populations without either one generalizing to the
   105	other.
   106	
   107	**Example** — A mid-fall-camp week showing a player's resting HR up 6 bpm over four days,
   108	alongside self-reported fatigue and soreness climbing, would meet Issurin's stated early-warning
   109	pattern for overtraining even before any blood marker moved. Per the Hooper et al. case,
   110	that combination of signals, not a lab panel, is what caught it in the cited study.

    12	---
    13	
    14	# Competing While Fatigued Erased Popov's Aerobic-Threshold Gains Within Days
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Issurin addresses whether competitions inside a training stage (not the
    17	final target competition) help or hurt (PDF pp. 128-129, printed pp. 117-118). His position:
    18	mid- and low-level competitions inside accumulation or transmutation mesocycles add useful
    19	emotional diversity and elicit training responses that enrich adaptation, but highly intense
    20	competitive efforts also trigger a stress-hormone response (catecholamines, cortisol) that
    21	reinforces the catabolic process (Viru & Viru, 2001), can reduce muscle mass and maximal
    22	strength, and, the specific mechanism named here, suppresses aerobic-enzyme activity and
    23	mitochondrial oxidative capacity (Volkov, 1986), shortening the residual training effect of the
    24	preceding mesocycle (citing Issurin & Lustig, 2004, the same paper behind
    25	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]). The supporting case: Alexander
    26	Popov's (Russia, multi-Olympic/World swimming champion) preparation was tracked with an
    27	incremental stepwise swimming test measuring anaerobic threshold speed (blood lactate = 4 mM)
    28	and the speed producing 8 mM lactate (the stated lower limit of highly intense glycolytic work).
    29	Measurements were taken at the start of a highly concentrated aerobic mesocycle, again 10 days
    30	later, and again a few days after Popov competed several times (Figure 3.11, PDF p. 129,
    31	printed p. 118; verified against page image, adapted from Pyne & Touretski, 1993). Both
    32	velocity markers rose substantially over the mesocycle's first 10 days, then **fell
    33	substantially** after the competition. Issurin attributes this decline directly to the
    34	competition-shortened residual, not to any change in training content.
    35	
    36	**Why it works — the author's own attributed mechanism, not independently re-derived here** —
    37	Issurin's stated chain is: highly intense competitive effort triggers a stress-hormone response
    38	that suppresses aerobic-enzyme and mitochondrial activity (citing Volkov, 1986), which is the
    39	same physiological substrate underlying aerobic endurance's normal ~30-day residual
    40	(see [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]), so a hard competition
    41	acts like an accelerant on that decay clock rather than a separate, independent event.
    42	
    43	**When to apply** — As a citable, named-athlete illustration for why a program including
    44	in-season or in-training-stage competitive tests should expect some real cost to basic-ability
    45	residuals, not treat competing as a free additional training stimulus. Directly supports the
    46	caution already logged for the transmutation mesocycle
    47	(see [[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]) about why
    48	"including competition" is listed as an *option*, with tradeoffs, rather than an unqualified
    49	recommendation. **Inference:** for football, this is a reason to expect that a physically
    50	brutal, high-intensity early-season or mid-season game can measurably eat into whatever aerobic
    51	or strength base was built in the preceding weeks, not just add acute fatigue that resolves in
    52	a few days, which argues for the mini-block "topping up" logic in
    53	[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]] being applied proactively after
    54	unusually hard, high-intensity games, not only on a fixed calendar schedule.
    55	
    56	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a single elite swimmer's data, reported secondhand
    57	(Pyne & Touretski, 1993, published via Issurin & Lustig, 2004), with no comparison athlete who
    58	trained the same mesocycle without competing, and no statistical test of the pre/post-competition
    59	change reported in this text: the chart (Figure 3.11) shows one athlete's trajectory, not a
    60	group result. **Inference:** swimming's anaerobic-threshold/lactate-based test protocol has no
    61	direct football analog; football has no simple single-modality repeated field test that isolates
    62	"aerobic threshold" the way a stepwise swim test does, so this exact monitoring approach cannot
    63	be copied, only the underlying caution (hard competition costs some residual) can be carried
    64	over. This case does not address whether the effect is dose-dependent on competition intensity,
    65	duration, or the athlete's fitness level entering the competition.
    66	
    67	**Example** — A strength staff noting that a physically demanding, high-effort game (e.g., a
    68	triple-overtime contest, or a game following an unusually taxing travel/short-week schedule)
    69	likely cost the team some of the conditioning base built the prior weeks has a named precedent
    70	(Popov's threshold-speed decline) for treating that as a real, not just anecdotal, training-load
    71	event worth a deliberate light aerobic "top-up" in the following week, rather than assuming a
    72	normal recovery day fully addresses it.
    73	
    74	**Related** — [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
    75	[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]],
    76	[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]],
    77	[[case-study--popov-aerobic-strength-microcycle]].

    12	---
    13	
    14	# When a Training Stage Outruns the 30-Day Residual Clock, Insert a Mini-Block, Don't Just Add Workouts
    15	
    16	**What it is** — This section directly answers the mismatch already flagged in
    17	[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]: the accumulation
    18	mesocycle's basic-ability residual runs out at about **30 days** (Table 1.6; see
    19	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]), which caps how long the
    20	following transmutation-plus-realization stretch can run before basic abilities decay below
    21	target. But Issurin notes many sports need their transmutation mesocycle to run **3-4 weeks**
    22	for anaerobic glycolytic development, and the realization mesocycle (taper) can run **about two
    23	weeks**: together, roughly **five weeks**, which already exceeds the ~30-day strength-aerobic
    24	residual (PDF pp. 129-130, printed pp. 118-119; verified against page image). Issurin's stated
    25	fix: do **not** simply add extra aerobic or strength workouts into the transmutation mesocycle
    26	to "top up" the decaying residual. This fails because the highly intense transmutation
    27	mesocycle actively suppresses the immediate effect of aerobic training, and the anabolic
    28	strength stimulus needs recovery time the transmutation mesocycle cannot spare. Instead, insert
    29	a **special compact mini-block (a short microcycle)** dedicated to the decaying ability. Figure
    30	3.12 (PDF p. 130, printed p. 119; verified against page image) diagrams the resulting pattern
    31	for a training stage, in sequence: **accumulation** (high-volume basic aerobic-strength
    32	workloads, **20-25 days**), then **transmutation** (highly intensive specific workloads,
    33	**20-25 days**, with a **mini-block** insertion partway through), then **realization** (taper
    34	and maximal speed, **10-16 days**), then **competition**. Issurin gives a worked contrast of two
    35	real scheduling situations (PDF p. 131, printed p. 120): when two targeted competitions are only
    36	**five to six weeks apart** (his cited example: kayaking's European and World Championships),
    37	the fix is to compress the whole stage (10-14 days accumulation, 10-14 days transmutation, 8-10
    38	days realization), short enough that the accumulation mesocycle's own residual still covers the
    39	whole stage, so **no mini-block is needed at all**. When circumstances instead force a longer,
    40	**7-9 week** training stage (his example: pre-Olympic preparation, where the international
    41	calendar has no tune-up competitions before the Games), the recommended answer is to plan longer
    42	mesocycles **and** include the mini-block, because a stage that long cannot otherwise carry the
    43	accumulation-phase residual all the way to competition. The chapter's own summary restates the
    44	placement rule concretely: an **aerobic mini-block can be inserted inside the transmutation
    45	mesocycle**, and a **highly intense anaerobic mini-block can be inserted inside the realization
    46	mesocycle** (PDF p. 132, printed p. 121): each mesocycle gets a short dose of whichever
    47	ability it does not otherwise train, timed to arrive before that ability's own residual clock
    48	runs out.
    49	
    50	**Why it works** — The reasoning is entirely about matching mini-block placement to what a
    51	normal workout addition cannot achieve: a single or a few extra sessions of the decaying
    52	modality, embedded inside a mesocycle whose entire design is optimized for a *different*
    53	ability, gets swallowed by that mesocycle's dominant physiological demand (suppressed
    54	aerobic adaptation under transmutation's glycolytic load; insufficient recovery for anabolic
    55	strength work under either mesocycle's fatigue). A discrete mini-block, by contrast, is
    56	short enough to insert without abandoning the surrounding mesocycle's main purpose, but is its
    57	own coherent unit (its own brief loading-then-recovery structure) rather than scattered
    58	single sessions, which is why Issurin insists on "not several additional workouts but a
    59	special compact mini-block."
    60	
    61	**When to apply — this is the entry most directly responsive to the strength-and-conditioning
    62	miss-log's "peaking phase structure for collegiate football" gap (logged 2026-09-03), and the
    63	clearest football calendar mapping in this chapter — Inference throughout** —
    64	
    65	- **The gap between the final regular-season or conference-championship game and a bowl game**
    66	  (commonly roughly 3-6 weeks depending on bowl selection and game date) is structurally the
    67	  same scheduling decision Issurin poses in his worked example. A **short** gap (roughly
    68	  5-6 weeks or less) should be handled like his compressed-stage case: run a short
    69	  accumulation-transmutation-realization sequence sized to fit inside the gap (e.g., 10-14 days
    70	  rebuild / 10-14 days sharpen / remaining days as realization/taper), in which case a
    71	  strength-aerobic residual built at the very start plausibly survives to the bowl game without
    72	  needing a mini-block. A **longer** gap (closer to 6+ weeks, which happens for some
    73	  earlier-selected bowls) more closely resembles his 7-9 week pre-Olympic case: plan a longer
    74	  rebuild phase **and** insert an aerobic (or strength) mini-block partway through the
    75	  bowl-prep transmutation-equivalent work, specifically to protect the basic conditioning base
    76	  built early in the gap from decaying below target by game day.
    77	- **In-season, week to week:** [[case-study--popov-competition-shortens-residual-effects]]
    78	  already shows that a hard game can itself accelerate residual decay; a bye week, or a week
    79	  after an unusually taxing game, is a natural, calendar-given opportunity to run something like
    80	  Issurin's aerobic mini-block (a few days of concentrated aerobic-strength work) to "top up" a
    81	  basic-ability residual before it drops further, rather than treating every week's training
    82	  content as identical regardless of how the prior weeks' games affected the athletes.
    83	- **Eric's baseline** does not currently name a mini-block concept or an explicit bowl-prep
    84	  periodization structure at all; this framework is the single most direct, numerically specific
    85	  answer this ingest has produced to that gap, and should be flagged to Eric as a candidate
    86	  structure to react to, not an already-adopted practice.
    87	
    88	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — **Population caveat, repeated deliberately because this is
    89	the chapter's central prescriptive claim:** every piece of evidence behind this framework
    90	(the 30-day residual table, the kayaking/pre-Olympic worked examples, the Popov case) comes from
    91	individual, endurance-or-technical Olympic sports with a fixed, known international competition
    92	calendar set months or years in advance. Football's bowl-selection process is itself uncertain
    93	until late in the season (a team does not always know its exact bowl date and opponent far in
    94	advance), which makes pre-planning an exact-length rebuild-then-taper sequence harder than in
    95	Issurin's kayaking example, where the championship dates are fixed well ahead of the season.
    96	**Inference:** none of Issurin's specific day-counts (20-25 / 20-25 / 10-16 days; the 5-6 week
    97	vs. 7-9 week contrast) were derived from or tested against a team-contact-sport calendar; they
    98	should be treated as a structural template to adapt to football's specific bowl-selection
    99	timeline and roster fatigue state at season's end (which is itself compounded by an already-long
   100	season, unlike Issurin's examples where the "prior mesocycle" is a dedicated, undisturbed
   101	accumulation block rather than 12+ weeks of in-season competition). The mini-block's own
   102	duration is not specified numerically in this section (Issurin calls it a "short microcycle,"
   103	consistent with the 2-4 day aerobic contrast mini-block already given in
   104	[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]'s Table 3.10):
   105	treat 2-4 days as the applicable figure by cross-reference, not as independently stated here.
   106	
   107	**Example** — For a 4-week gap between a team's last game and its bowl game, a plan following
   108	this framework could run roughly 10-12 days rebuilding aerobic-strength base (accumulation),
   109	10-12 days of sharpened, game-plan-specific and higher-intensity work (transmutation) with a
   110	short 2-3 day aerobic mini-block inserted partway through that phase to protect the just-rebuilt
   111	base, then a final 7-10 days as a realization/taper phase per
   112	[[framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]], versus a 6-week gap, where the
   113	accumulation and transmutation phases could each extend closer to Issurin's 20-25 day figures,
   114	still with the mini-block insertion, since a stage that long cannot otherwise be covered by a
   115	single unbroken residual window.
   116	
   117	**Related** — [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
   118	[[framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]],
   119	[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]],
   120	[[framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]],
   121	[[case-study--popov-competition-shortens-residual-effects]],
   122	[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]].

    83	- **Eric's baseline** does not currently name a mini-block concept or an explicit bowl-prep
    84	  periodization structure at all; this framework is the single most direct, numerically specific
    85	  answer this ingest has produced to that gap, and should be flagged to Eric as a candidate
    86	  structure to react to, not an already-adopted practice.
    87	
    88	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — **Population caveat, repeated deliberately because this is
    89	the chapter's central prescriptive claim:** every piece of evidence behind this framework
    90	(the 30-day residual table, the kayaking/pre-Olympic worked examples, the Popov case) comes from
    91	individual, endurance-or-technical Olympic sports with a fixed, known international competition
    92	calendar set months or years in advance. Football's bowl-selection process is itself uncertain
    93	until late in the season (a team does not always know its exact bowl date and opponent far in
    94	advance), which makes pre-planning an exact-length rebuild-then-taper sequence harder than in
    95	Issurin's kayaking example, where the championship dates are fixed well ahead of the season.
    96	**Inference:** none of Issurin's specific day-counts (20-25 / 20-25 / 10-16 days; the 5-6 week
    97	vs. 7-9 week contrast) were derived from or tested against a team-contact-sport calendar; they
    98	should be treated as a structural template to adapt to football's specific bowl-selection
    99	timeline and roster fatigue state at season's end (which is itself compounded by an already-long
   100	season, unlike Issurin's examples where the "prior mesocycle" is a dedicated, undisturbed
   101	accumulation block rather than 12+ weeks of in-season competition). The mini-block's own
   102	duration is not specified numerically in this section (Issurin calls it a "short microcycle,"
   103	consistent with the 2-4 day aerobic contrast mini-block already given in
   104	[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]'s Table 3.10):
   105	treat 2-4 days as the applicable figure by cross-reference, not as independently stated here.
   106	
   107	**Example** — For a 4-week gap between a team's last game and its bowl game, a plan following
   108	this framework could run roughly 10-12 days rebuilding aerobic-strength base (accumulation),
   109	10-12 days of sharpened, game-plan-specific and higher-intensity work (transmutation) with a
   110	short 2-3 day aerobic mini-block inserted partway through that phase to protect the just-rebuilt
   111	base, then a final 7-10 days as a realization/taper phase per
   112	[[framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]], versus a 6-week gap, where the
   113	accumulation and transmutation phases could each extend closer to Issurin's 20-25 day figures,
   114	still with the mini-block insertion, since a stage that long cannot otherwise be covered by a
   115	single unbroken residual window.
   116

C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\periodization--bompa\heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio.md:22:**When NOT to apply** — The 3:1 figure is a rule of thumb, not a constant. Training type shifts it — anaerobic work is more fatiguing and lengthens the ratio; CNS-intensive work can extend fatigue well past 24 hr. Don't use it to schedule to the hour. Pairs with [[principle--supercompensation-cycle]] and [[framework--three-training-effects]].
C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\periodization--bompa\framework--three-training-effects.md:22:**When NOT to apply** — Don't judge a program by immediate-effect readings alone (a fatigued, depressed test mid-block is expected, not failure). The cumulative effect requires deliberate alternation of load and recovery — pile on intensity without compensation and you get overtraining, not a rebound. See [[heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]] and [[principle--supercompensation-cycle]].
C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\periodization--bompa\principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching.md:20:**When to apply** — Advanced athletes who can tolerate high loads; building a potent stimulus before a taper/peak; reducing long-term work volume versus concurrent training; timing a delayed performance rebound to a competition window.
C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\periodization--bompa\principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching.md:22:**When NOT to apply** — Not for novices or athletes without the training capacity to absorb saturating loads — fatigue is substantial during accumulation and mismanagement tips into overtraining. The delayed-rebound timing (4–12 wk) must be planned backward from competition, or the peak lands in the wrong week. Builds on [[principle--supercompensation-cycle]] and [[framework--step-loading-paradigm]]; bounded by [[principle--individualization]].
C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\periodization--bompa\framework--step-loading-paradigm.md:18:**Why it works** — Loading accumulates fatigue across the three steps; the unloading week sheds fatigue, raises preparedness, and lets the supercompensation/adaptation surface before the next overload (see [[principle--supercompensation-cycle]], [[heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]]). It operationalizes progressive overload safely (see [[principle--progressive-overload-threshold]]). The more progressive loading steps, the longer the unloading needed.
C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\periodization--bompa\principle--progressive-overload-threshold.md:22:**When NOT to apply** — Not a license for linear, monotonic load increase indefinitely — that path leads to the maladaptation branch. The *rate* and *form* of progression must respect recovery and training age. Overload without adequate recovery is how you cross into overreaching. Pairs with [[principle--supercompensation-cycle]] (recovery side) and is bounded by [[heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]].

# The Two-Factor Model Can Be Formalized Mathematically, and Its Research Base Argues Against Heavy Training Right Before Competition

**What it is** — The Two-Factor (Fitness-Fatigue) Model treats preparedness at time t as
initial preparedness plus the summed effect of a slow-decaying fitness after-effect and a
faster-decaying fatigue after-effect, each with its own magnitude and decay-time constant
(Banister et al., 1992). Banister and Calvert (1980) originated this with the Training
Impulse (TRIMP), a quantified unit of training load used to model and predict elite
swimming performance from the fitness/fatigue balance. Zatsiorsky (1995) is cited for the
same 3:1 fitness-to-fatigue decay ratio already in this library's Bompa material. Later
research building on this model examined tapering specifically: Fitz-Clarke et al. (1991)
found presently accepted taper protocols may be too rigorous and short for best results,
and several studies (Zarkadas et al. 1995; Mujika et al. 1996; Shepley et al. 1992) found
that proper placement of training volume during a taper is a key optimization factor, with
high training volume in the days immediately preceding competition possibly detrimental to
performance. Different muscle groups recover heterochronically, which is why some Russian
restoration specialists deliberately avoid applying restorative methods (e.g. massage) to
every muscle group after every session, since supercompensation is reportedly more
pronounced with partial rather than total restoration. (PDF pp. 99-100, printed pp. 88-89.)

**Why it works** — Modeling preparedness as the sum of two exponentially-decaying
after-effects with different time constants gives periodization a quantitative structure
(not just a qualitative "wave" description), which is what allows taper researchers to ask
a specific, testable question: how much and how recently loaded should training be before
competition to maximize the fitness-minus-fatigue difference at competition time.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the more technical, equation-based underpinning
of this library's already-captured practical rule
([[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]]); cite this entry when a
more rigorous or quantitative framing is needed (e.g. explaining the model to a sport
scientist or in a research-facing document), and cite the Bompa heuristic for the everyday
coaching rule of thumb. The taper-volume finding directly supports reducing training
volume, not just intensity, in the days immediately before a competition or key testing
date.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific mathematical constants (A, B, T1, T2)
must be fit per individual and per training phase, and the text notes they require
periodic re-estimation; do not treat this as a plug-and-play formula without that
fitting process. Inference: the cited taper studies are 1990s endurance-sport studies
(Shepley et al. 1992, middle-distance runners; Zarkadas et al. 1995, triathletes; Mujika et
al. 1996, swimmers; the text itself does not name the sports studied); don't assume the
exact taper-volume findings transfer unchanged to football or other team sports without
independent verification.

**Example** — **Inference:** rather than assuming a flat "taper week" cuts intensity but
keeps volume similar, this model's logic and the cited taper research both point toward
deliberately reducing volume (not just easing intensity) in the final days before a key
competition or test date, to let the longer-lasting fitness effect show through as the
shorter fatigue effect clears.

**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]],
[[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]].

# "Adaptive Reconstruction" vs. "Supercompensation": Verkhoshansky/Siff's Sharper Critique

**What it is** — The authors argue "adaptive reconstruction" is a more accurate term than
"supercompensation" for the body's response to training load. One reason is stated
directly alongside the term: enhanced performance "is not simply the result of increased
stores of bioenergetic substances, but also of structural changes in muscle and other
tissues, as well as enhanced efficiency and rates of bioenergetic and neuromuscular
processing" (printed 84). A second reason comes not from that passage but from the
separate single-factor-model critique in 1.16.3: ATP "has never been shown to deplete
significantly, even after very strenuous exercise," and "no supercompensation has yet been
observed to occur among any of the other biochemicals" besides glycogen; each substance
returns to its initial level on its own timeline, so "the timing of subsequent loads to
stimulate the appropriate type of supercompensation remains indeterminate" (printed 87-88).

- Daily subjective wellness surveys, rolled out across multiple sports via the AMS app starting summer 2022, were abandoned after roughly one academic year because athletes learned to game the consistent, low-effort answers the survey rewarded; the data looked clean but carried no real signal. Wellness surveys are still used, deliberately, in return-to-play scenarios and with athletes managing chronic health conditions, where subjective context still adds value objective data can't supply. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
## Tensions and contradictions

1. **The task's own premise doesn't fully hold.** Both class transcripts (Class 1 and Class 3) are diarized entirely under a single Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line — including Class 3, which the Spring 2026 teaching schedule assigns solo to Rash (`spring-2026-teaching.md`: "Feb. 5 | Conditioning - Alactic-Aerobic | Rash"). Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name instead of doing real per-speaker diarization. content.content: Physiological and mood state parameters were monitored during a 6-month swimming season in an attempt to determine markers of overtraining and recovery. Fourteen elite male and female swimmers were tested early-, mid-, and late-season and shortly before and after major competition. Training details and subjective ratings of well-being were compiled by the athletes in daily logs. Three swimmers were classified as stale based upon performance deterioration and prolonged, high fatigue levels. Staleness scores were calculated for each athlete using performance change from early- to late-season and daily fatigue ratings for the season. Regression analysis revealed a battery of well-being ratings which predicted staleness scores, accounting for 76% of the variance. The late-season stress ratings and plasma catecholamine levels at rest predicted staleness scores, accounting for 85% of the variance. During tapering, well-being ratings predicted improvement in competitive performance, accounting for 72% of the variance of the improvement in race times from previous best times. It was concluded that self-reported ratings of well-being may provide an efficient means of monitoring both overtraining and recovery; plasma catecholamine levels at rest may provide an additional objective tool for diagnosis.

content.content:
--- Is testosterone influencing explosive performance? The primary objective of this study was to analyze the relationship between testosterone levels and vertical jumping performance in elite men and women athletes. The secondary objective was to verify whether testosterone levels and vertical jumping performance were different in men and women athletes and if those measurements were different between different athletic groups. Seventy (22 women and 48 men) elite athletes in track and field (sprinters), handball, volleyball, and soccer competing at national and international levels participated in the study. After 10 hours of fasting and 1 day of rest, blood samples were drawn from the antecubital vein for determining testosterone levels. Vertical jumping tests consisted of countermovement jumps conducted on a resistive platform connected to a digital timer. Resting testosterone levels in women were 9.5% of those of the men (respectively 0.62 +/- 0.06 ng.ml(-1) and 6.49 +/- 0.37 ng.ml(-1); p < 0.001). Countermovement jump performance was significantly different between women and men athletes, with women's jumping ability 86.3% of that of men (p < 0.001). A significant positive relationship was identified between testosterone levels and vertical jump performance when all data where considered (r = 0.61, p < 0.001, n = 70). --- Antioxidant supplementation and tapering exercise improve exercise-induced antioxidant response.

Objective and methods

The present controlled-training, double-blind study (supplemented, n = 7; placebo, n = 9) investigated whether taper training (TT) and antioxidant supplementation, i.e., 150 micro g of selenium, 2000 IU of retinol, 120 mg of ascorbic acid and 30 IU of alpha-tocopherol, modulates antioxidant potential, redox status and oxidative damage occurrence both at rest and in response to exercise. Two weeks of TT followed four weeks of overloaded training. Dietary intakes were recorded. Before and after TT, triathletes did a duathlon consisting of 5-km run, 20-km bike and 5-km run. Biological studies were conducted at rest and after exercise.

Results

Whatever the nutritional status, TT induced a decrease in resting blood reduced glutathione (GSH) concentration (p < 0.001), erythrocyte superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity (p < 0.0001) and plasma total antioxidant status (TAS) (p < 0.05). Only in the supplemented group (Su) with TT, did plasma glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px) activity decrease (p < 0.05) and CD4(+) cell concentration increase (p < 0.05). However, antioxidant supplementation increased plasma TAS increase in response to exercise and TT (p < 0.05). After exercise, TT also induced a lower decrease in blood reduced and oxidized (GSSG) glutathione (p < 0.01) in both groups, but TT had no effect on lipoperoxidation as estimated by plasma thiobarbituric reactive substances or on muscular damage occurrence estimated by plasma creatine kinase isoenzyme MB mass.

Conclusion

During TT, antioxidant supplementation at nutritional doses reinforces antioxidant status response to exercise, with an effect on exercise-induced oxidative stress, and no effect on oxidative damage.

+# The Five-Element Case-Review Structure

+**What it is** — Harries reviews each of his four case studies through the same five elements, stated explicitly: "the rehab timeline, which is a high-level overview of the return to play calendar"; "the loading structure. So how was loading planned and how was it progressed across on-field rehab"; "the progression of maximum velocity and how those linear running intensities were increased"; "our multi-directional speed and agility progressions and how we developed acceleration, deceleration and change of direction"; and "for each case study... the sport-specific skill progressions and how the technical and tactical tasks were integrated" (~00:39-01:17). He also states the cases were deliberately chosen to minimize individual complexity so the framework's application would read clearly, while acknowledging "no case is ever entirely free from complexity" (~01:21-01:45), and that he included cases that "didn't go perfect to show that the real world is not always that way" (~01:45-01:51).
+**Why it works** — No stated mechanism; this is a presentation and documentation structure Harries uses for teaching, not a claim about rehab physiology or efficacy.

+**When to apply** — As a template for a Baylor RTP case log or after-action review: for a returning athlete, record (1) the RTP timeline/calendar, (2) the loading structure and how it was progressed, (3) max-velocity progression, (4) MDSA progression, and (5) sport-skill progression. Eric's baseline: `method-baseline.md` records that standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates "do not yet exist" at Applied Performance and are named as unfinished Phase 2 work; this five-element structure is a ready-made scaffold specifically for RTP case documentation, distinct from that broader reporting gap.

+**When NOT to apply** — This is a presentation structure built for four selected, deliberately simplified cases, not a validated clinical documentation standard, and Harries does not claim it captures everything relevant to an actual RTP decision. It has no explicit slot for the competitive-exposure/hesitation criteria in [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]] and [[heuristic--hesitation-signals-unready-but-is-unmeasured]] (those show up folded into the sport-skill-progression element in practice, not as their own listed element). Do not treat the five elements as exhaustive without adding Baylor's own required documentation fields (medical clearance sign-off, testing-battery results, incident/mechanism detail) alongside them.

+**Example** — Each of the four case-study entries in this folder already follows this five-element order in its own body sections (rehab timeline in "What it is," then loading structure, MV progression, MDSA, sport-specific skill as separate paragraphs), though none names the structure explicitly; see [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] for the clearest example.

+**Related** — [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]; [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]]; [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]; [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] (reciprocal link suggestion: each could add "documented using [[framework--five-element-case-review-structure]]" to its own Related line)

# Review: Issurin, *Block Periodization* (2008), Chapter 3 (Opus falsification pass, round 1)

Reviewer: Claude Opus 5.5, 2026-09-27. Brief: `staging/review_book_prompt.md` plus `docs/ATOMIZE_BRIEF.md`.
Scope: the 12 entries in `staging/_scope_issurin_ch3.txt` (folder `staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/block-periodization--issurin/`). The Ch1-2 entries were read for duplicates and contradictions only, not graded.
Source: `Block Periodization - Issurin.pdf`. Chapter 3 (idx 87-135, printed 76-124) was extracted in full with PyMuPDF and read. Every table and figure cited by an in-scope entry was rendered and read as a page image: Tables 3.1, 3.4, 3.5, 3.7, 3.12, 3.13; Figures 3.4, 3.5, 3.7, 3.8, 3.10, 3.11 and 3.12 (3.12 zoomed).
Primary-source spot checks: I pulled the Europe PMC abstracts for three studies the chapter retells: Hooper et al. 1995, Cardinale & Stone 2006 and Margaritis et al. 2003.

## Locator convention

- Entries cite the **0-based PDF index = printed + 11**. That holds on every Ch3 page. A viewer shows printed + 12. Below, "idx N / p.M" means index N, printed page M.
- Only one entry locator is wrong: the Cardinale & Stone case is on **idx 104 / p.93**, not idx 103 / p.92. All other page locators check out.

## Global findings (apply across rows; not repeated per row)

- **G1 Unlabelled writer voice (recurring from Ch1).** Every **Example** in scope is an invented football or Baylor scenario, or a generic walk-through, with no "Inference:" prefix. The "Population caveat:" paragraphs are unlabelled too, and so are the "this is the entry most directly answering the miss-log gap" openers. Most of these are reasonable; they just need the label. The "Inference, mapped to a college football calendar" headers are correctly labelled, which is an improvement on Ch1.
- **G2 Em dashes: clean.** The only em dashes are the house-style bold section headers. The Ch1 body-prose problem did not recur.
- **G3 False "verified against page image" stamps.** Four entries (and `_book.md`) claim page-image verification for content that the page image contradicts:
  - Figure 3.7: the entry inverts the AM/PM content.
  - Table 3.7: the "3-6 days" comment belongs to the Impact row, not Restoration.
  - Figure 3.10: the figure shows expenditure falling **to** about 69%. The text says "by up to 69.3%".
  - Figure 3.11: the entry's title says the gains were "erased", but both markers stay above baseline.

  `_book.md` says all Ch3 tables and figures "matched exactly". That is false; correct it when these rows are fixed.
- **G4 The Issurin 2016 vault brief is still unlinked.** No Ch3 entry links `research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-...md`. Its line 57 ("does not supply validated block durations or effect estimates for collegiate American football") and line 58 (the multi-targeted conclusion "should not be treated as settled comparative evidence") belong in When NOT for the accumulation, transmutation, realization and prolonging entries.
- **G5 Supercompensation as the taper mechanism.** The pre-competitive and realization entries both rest "Why it works" on supercompensation (idx 106 / p.95; idx 122 / p.111). That is the author's stated mechanism, so plain text is correct. Both entries should add `[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]` (staging, `contested`) to Related.
- **Confidence:** no `proven` rating is used anywhere in scope. The three case studies are correctly `untested`. The framework entries are at the `supported` ceiling. The one `contested` entry (transmutation) is mis-grounded; see its row.

## Entry table

Severity tags: **[major]** means the source is misstated in substance; **[minor]** means a locator, wording, omission or labelling problem.

| File | Verdict | Problem (entry vs source, with page) | Exact correction |
|---|---|---|---|

The book restricts one-peak designs to "sufficiently prepared high-performance athletes but not ... novice and less prepared athletes" (idx 90 / p.79). It proposes the 5-point scale precisely for "non-measurable sports like sailing or team and dual sports" (idx 89 / p.78), and Fig 3.2's last session can be "a match in team or dual sports" (idx 91 / p.80). (2) When to apply calls "a normal in-season game week" Issurin's **competitive** microcycle. Table 3.1 defines that type as "participation in competition", with high to very high load (idx 88 / p.77). The book treats the in-season team week as a separate design (3.1.7, idx 108 / p.97). (3) Why it works credits the peak-trough logic to the concentration principle (writer synthesis). The author's own reason is on idx 90 / p.79: "The two or three load reductions facilitate athletes' restoration and stimulate their readiness to effectively perform subsequent high demand workouts." (4) The entry omits that the impact microcycle needs a special restoration program (diet, supplements, hydrotherapy, massage, relaxation) (idx 89 / p.78). (5) The "impact week concept sometimes used informally" is an uncited general claim. (6) Example unlabelled (G1).
